The World Health Organization says a possible case of pneumonic plague in Russia presents a “very low” risk outside the country as investigators look into what caused the death from pneumonia of a lab employee there last week.
The U.N. health agency said on Tuesday that it has been in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
The case and the investigation, led by Russian officials, have revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab. WHO has not provided a definitive answer to how the pandemic began.
Here's what to know about the case and how experts are mobilizing after the woman's death:
Pneumonic plague is a form of the disease that affects the lungs
The incubation period for pneumonic plague — which means lung-based and is the most virulent form of the disease — can be as short as 24 hours, according to WHO. It’s a less common but severe form that can spread between people through respiratory particles.
If untreated, the illness can be fatal, but recovery rates are high if detected and treated in time — within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms, WHO says.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often involving the coughing up of blood.
The more common form of plague — bubonic plague — is caused by the bite of an infected flea, and can develop into open sores filled with pus.
Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that is mostly caused by viruses or bacteria, and is spread generally through contact with infected people or from airborne droplets. WHO says pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
A look at what Russian officials are saying about the case
Through an international health alert system, Russian health officials on Tuesday said a full range of preventive measures had been carried out — including tracing of the deceased woman's contacts, medical monitoring and lab tests.
“Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens in any of the contacts,” said the note from Russian authorities, which was relayed to The Associated Press by WHO.
"Based on available data, laboratory test results, and health status, medical monitoring for 100% of the contacts has now been concluded," it said. “The epidemiological situation is stable and remains under monitoring.”
The woman died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside the city of Irkutsk, and its mayor said the hospital was placed under quarantine. The top officials from Russia’s national public health watchdog traveled to the region on Friday.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov advised the public to follow official statements from the watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumors or speculation.”
WHO has mobilized its own experts to look into the case
WHO spokesman Christian Lindmeier told a U.N. briefing on Tuesday that the institute where the woman worked “studies dangerous pathogens,” including plague in a part of Siberia where the disease "occurs naturally in wild animals.”
He said Russian officials have not yet asked for WHO experts to deploy to Russia, where authorities are "looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”
In recent days, WHO has brought in technical experts to its Geneva headquarters and the European regional office in Copenhagen in connection with the investigation, including specialists in high-threat pathogens.
“The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates ... the risk to be moderate-to-low for Irkutsk; a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole; and very low for the WHO European region,” Lindmeier said.
Trump and Rubio have commented on the case
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he was watching the situation with concern and that the United States would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case.
Asked about Trump’s remarks, Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Tuesday that “it is always very good when mutual assistance is offered.” He wouldn’t elaborate further, deferring to Rospotrebnadzor.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russian authorities to share more information.
“Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” he said at a news conference in Iceland. “We’re watching it very closely and I think the whole world is watching it very closely."
“We encourage Russia to be more transparent and share more information with the world,” Rubio said, adding this has so far been “quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.”
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia,” although because of modern living conditions and antibiotics, its potential was limited.
Dr. Glenn Wortmann, at the MedStar Washington Hospital Center, said the bacteria that cause plague don't “travel very far” and a person would “really need to be face-to-face” with an infected person to get pneumonic plague.
“The chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen, not with this type of bacteria, because it’s not spread easily and we have antibiotics to stop it from spreading,” he added.
Associated Press writers Dasha Litvinova in Tallinn, Estonia, and Matthew Lee in Reykjavik, Iceland, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: France's Mistral launches AI model it says outperforms some Chinese rivals
articles.title_zh: France's Mistral launches AI model it says outperforms some Chinese rivals
articles.content_orig:
Mistral on Tuesday unveiled a new AI model it said ranked among the best open models in the world, as Western companies race to close the capability gap with Chinese developers in the market.
Mistral Large 4 (ML4), also known as le Chonk, is a 1-trillion-parameter model that is particularly effective at tasks related to cyber, coding, manufacturing, finance and multimodal, the French company said.
Long considered Europe's only answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral raised a 3 billion euros ($3.4 billion) Series D in September at a 21 billion euro valuation. The round cemented the company's status as one of the best-funded and most valuable AI startups in the region.
Access to so-called open AI models — the most capable of which have been Chinese — has become a key flashpoint in the intensifying race for technological supremacy between the U.S. and China.
Open AI models can be modified and self-hosted, in contrast to leading closed systems produced by OpenAI and Anthropic. Chinese open models are increasingly being adopted around the world.
Mistral Large 4 is being launched in preview to developers and "cybersecurity leaders," alongside state authorities, before it is released more widely later this month, the company said.
ML4 was trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months that were deployed in Mistral's own data centers in Europe.
When its core parameters are released, ML4 will rank among the top open-weight models globally on aggregate benchmark performance, Mistral said in a statement. The company added that ML4 was the strongest open-weight model developed outside China by a "substantial margin."
The new model still lags behind the frontier in areas such as coding.
"The model capabilities will further improve as we scale up our training capacity, following our Series D fundraise," said Guillaume Lample, co-founder and chief scientist of Mistral.
"Further, the cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks," he added.
Open models were thrust into the spotlight earlier this year when it emerged that startup Hugging Face turned to Chinese-based Z.ai's GLM 5.2 to defend against a breach from rogue OpenAI agents. Hugging Face initially turned to leading U.S. closed systems to defend itself, but was blocked by guardrails that mistook its actions for an attack.
Nvidia-backed American startup Reflection AI unveiled its first open model on Monday, which it claimed matched the capability of GLM 5.2, which was surpassed by GLM 5.3 in August.

articles.title_orig: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Liu Cixin, Liu Zhenyun Headline China’s Rights Push
articles.title_zh: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Liu Cixin, Liu Zhenyun Headline China’s Rights Push
articles.content_orig:
Chinese publishers have often struggled to find audiences for their books in English. But this year, the Chinese delegation to the Frankfurt Book Fair is bringing samples of books by two of China’s best-known authors, science fiction writer Liu Cixin and novelist Liu Zhenyun, to sell rights.
Liu Cixin’s Hugo Award–winning Three-Body Problem trilogy has been a bestseller in English translation and has spawned a Netflix series, with the second and final season due to be released later this year. Phoenix Publishing and Yilin Press have been publishing the graphic novel adaptation of the Three-Body Problem trilogy, with the first volume, The Three-Body Problem, appearing last year; the second, The Dark Forest , hit bookstores in August; and the final book, Death’s End , is scheduled for August 2028. The books are illustrated by Wu Qingsong, a Golden Dragon Award–winning Chinese artist. The original trilogy—the first volume of which was published in 2006—has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide, according to Phoenix, and its first installment translated into English won the Hugo Award for best novel in 2015.
Rights for the graphic novel series have already been sold in France, Germany, Greece, Japan, Spain, and Turkey, and English-language samples will be available at the Phoenix stand at the fair. The book is being presented alongside a graphic novel adaptation of The Fire Keeper , which is described as Liu’s first children’s book, a science fiction fairy tale about young man who meets a fire keeper at the end of the world.
Another author with potential to become an international breakout star is Liu Zhenyun. Liu has published 12 books which have been translated into more than 30 languages, with some 15 million copies sold in China to date according to his publisher, People’s Literature Publishing House. He is wildly popular in China, where his 2009 novel Someone to Talk To sold more than 2.5 million copies, and where his 2012 novel I Did Not Kill My Husband sold nearly two million copies. Duke University Press published an English-language edition of Someone to Talk To in 2018, and Arcade Publishing released the English edition of I Did Not Kill My Husband in 2014.
Liu’s latest book, Salty Jokes , published by People’s Literature Publishing House, has already sold 1.1 million copies in China since its release last December. The novel is a black comedy about cancel culture, following the fall of an intellectual and former schoolteacher after an inappropriate relationship goes wrong and goes viral.
In China, Liu is nearly as famous as a pop star. Speaking with PW through an interpreter at the Beijing International Book Fair (BIBF) this past June, he described new levels of recognition in China: readers now approach him at train stations, airports, and restaurants for photos and autographs. “I regard them as gestures of kindness,” he said, adding that readers often annotate his books in the margins “sometimes with more words than what is printed on that single page” and occasionally draw maps of a novel’s characters. Critics in China have compared him to Balzac for his depiction of the collision of various strata of society.
To foster more translations from Chinese to English, U.K. consultancy Singing Grass and Paper Republic, an online magazine focused on Chinese literature in English, launched a new prize: the Voices of Today Literary Translation Prize. The intention was to promote the translation of more contemporary books, and the inaugural prize invited participants to translate an extract from Salty Jokes . More than 100 translators from 14 countries submitted work, and the winners were announced at the BIBF in June, with Australian Jenny Lu taking the top prize of £1,500 and two runners-up, Alexis Wu from the U.S. and Yaqi Xi from the U.K., each receiving £500. It is Lu’s sample translation that will be offered to publishers in Frankfurt.
Translator Nicky Harman, speaking for the judges, said, “We translators have waited a long time to see an international Chinese-to-English translation prize commensurate with the quality of translations coming out of the Sinophone world.” For his part, Liu Zhenyun praised the work and underscored how each translator offered different interpretations of the work, noting, in one seemingly simple example, that each rendered the name of a Chinese liquor similar to moonshine differently. The results ranged from “grain liquor” to “ration spirit” to “daily booze,” underscoring the importance of human translation in the age of AI. “A computer would likely only come up with one interpretation,” he told PW .

Jacob Kiplimo, at just 25-years-old, has had one of the best seasons in running history - and on Sunday, he could cap that off with a win and World Record at the 2026 Chicago Marathon .
Kiplimo currently holds a personal best of 2:00:28 over the full marathon distance, and he also has the half marathon World Record of 57:20 to his name - but more on that soon.
Australian, British, Irish and Canadian audiences can watch the Chicago Marathon LIVE on FloTrack
The Ugandan has had an unbelievable season so far in 2026. It all started at the 2026 World XC Championships where Kiplimo collected his third World XC Title in-a-row . He gapped Berihu Aregawi to win by 18-seconds in a statement victory.
Kiplimo then headed to Portugal in March. At the Lisbon Half Marathon, the young star set a World Record in the Half Marathon by posting a 57:20 for a 48-second victory.
Just over a month later, Kiplimo ran the 2026 London Marathon. In just his third race at the distance he finished third with an astounding 2:00:28. That race saw Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha run the two fastest times in World History.
But now - it may be Kiplimo's opportunity to raise the laurels in the Windy City.
It will be his first race since London - and the only thing holding him back may be the weather.
Conditions are expected to be a little warmer than expected for a mid-October race. Currently, temperatures are calling for Mid-60's, climbing up to the high 60's by the projected finish time around 9:30 AM. Humidity expected to be in the 50% to 60% range.
These conditions are outside of the optimal ranges for marathon running - but Kiplimo can certainly still prevail.
Amos Kipruto will stand as one of the toughest competitors in Sunday's field. Of Kenya, the 34 year old ran 2:01:39 to finish fourth behind Kiplimo at the 2026 London Marathon.
Kipruto has been a consistent contender on the World Major Marathon circuit this decade. He won London in 2022 and has sat on five World Major Podiums.
He is on a hot-streak in Chicago too. In 2024 his 2:04:50 earned him a third-place finish. Then in 2025 he upgraded to silver with a 2:03:54 effort.
Ethiopia's Milkesa Mengesha and Tadese Takele Bikila will also be in the mix. They both sport personal bests in the low-2:03's.
You also can't count out the Americans. Tough conditions could open the race up for Charles Hicks, Vinny Mauri, or Clayton Young. All will be gunning for the American Record of 2:04:43, which could spell an opportunity for an American to dip into the 2:03's.
Video footage from each event will be archived and stored in a video library for FloTrack subscribers to watch for the duration of their subscriptions.

articles.title_orig: 5 things to know about EU-China relations ahead of crucial talks
articles.title_zh: 5 things to know about EU-China relations ahead of crucial talks
articles.content_orig:
After months of tensions, relations between Brussels and Beijing are entering a crucial phase, with the European Commission having set October as a deadline to secure "tangible” results with Beijing to rebalance their trade relationship.
The stakes are high for the EU, whose trade deficit with China has now reached a record €1 billion a day.
Key talks will take place in Beijing at the end of this week between EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. They will be followed next week by a meeting of EU leaders, with China set to top the agenda.
For European policymakers, the diagnosis is increasingly clear: the situation is unsustainable, with a new wave of Chinese competition putting pressure on the EU’s industrial base two decades after China’s rapid economic expansion began — and putting thousands of jobs at risk.
“A massive industrial shock is affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.],” reads a Franco-German document which was sent on Monday to capitals and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Ahead of these crucial ten days, Euronews takes a deep dive into the EU-China relationship. Here are five things to know.
After several weeks of discussions held at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, Šefčovič will travel to Beijing on Thursday and Friday for high-level political discussions with Wentao.
Negotiations were launched last June, with the Europeans hoping to secure commitments from Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship. At the heart of the discussions is Chinese access to the EU market of 450 million consumers, with the Europeans seeking to protect EU industry from a wave of low-cost Chinese imports.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," EU Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné told Euronews in an exclusive interview three weeks ago, adding that the EU had already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year.
The Europeans also want to secure exports of rare earths from China, which are essential for EU industry, after Beijing blocked them amid a trade war with the US in 2025. Exports eventually resumed, but the truce runs only until 10 January 2027.
For the Commission, this week’s talks are essential, as EU leaders expect concrete results from the EU executive for their meeting next week.
EU member states’ approach to China has evolved since Germany came to recognise that its economy — the bloc’s largest — was increasingly exposed to Chinese competition. In 2024, Berlin opposed EU tariffs on low-cost Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). But in recent weeks, Germany has moved closer to France, which has taken a tougher stance and advocated stronger measures towards China.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called on Monday, in a letter to Commission President von der Leyen, for “the full use” of the EU’s existing trade defence instruments and for a “comprehensive framework” with new legal instruments.
In a document accompanying the letter, they listed proposals, including a new tool that would be in the hands of the Commission to allow a “decisive and systemic reaction,” including measures that could lead to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.”
The Commission would activate the tool unless a qualified majority voted against it. By introducing a reversed qualified majority voting system, the two leaders hope to make EU action easier and faster.
However, among member states, Madrid remains one of the most cautious towards China, despite having sought Chinese investment for several years.
Spain’s domestic political situation, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling for new elections, could nevertheless limit Madrid’s opposition to the EU’s strategy towards China.
Across Europe, European businesses are calling for tough action despite the risk of retaliation.
They want the EU not only to protect European industry through trade policy, but also to reduce its dependence on China, given the bloc’s critical vulnerabilities. Beijing demonstrated the risks of these dependencies in 2025, when it restricted exports of rare earths and chips essential to the automotive industry amid a dispute involving Dutch-based Nexperia.
The Federation of German Industries, the BDI, published a report on 25 September, saying that “systemic competition with China’s economy is increasingly calling into question the resilience of the open social market economy.”
It added: “Even if de-risking entails costs — including in the form of countermeasures — inaction would be significantly more costly economically in the long term and irresponsible from a security policy perspective.”
On 29 September, the Commission launched a consultation with EU businesses to help shape new measures, including a diversification tool aimed at addressing situations where reliance on a single supplier country poses a risk to the EU’s security of supply.
Since they began last June, negotiations between the Commission and Beijing have made little progress.
Beijing wants to maintain access to the EU market, while the Commission is seeking to negotiate import quotas by product. However, China holds important leverage in the talks, as it has a global monopoly on the production and processing of rare earths, which are key to the EU’s green tech, defence and car industries.
China already pushed back against a Commission proposal for “voluntary export restrictions” on EVs. On 20 September, a Chinese spokesperson said that such measures were contrary to the “principle of fair competition.”
"China's position is consistent. Any solution between China and the EU must ensure a balance of interests, comply with WTO rules and their respective domestic laws, and fully accommodate the interests of industries on both sides," the spokesperson said.
Tensions are mounting between the two sides, with both refraining from more aggressive moves.
Before negotiations started in June, the EU had already proposed the so-called Industrial Accelerator Act and the Cybersecurity Act, restricting access to the EU market for Chinese companies, with Beijing threatening of retaliation.
Since June, the Commission has continued to open probes into Chinese products over unfair trade practices, irritating Beijing, which over the summer forbade its companies from cooperating with Brussels on antitrust probes.
According to several people familiar with the matter, EU countries are also holding back the launch of an investigation into the chemicals sector that could lead to safeguards — tariffs and quotas.
Finally, last Saturday, China put pressure on the Europeans ahead of this week’s critical talks by launching an investigation into EU chemicals, suspecting dumping of EU p-nitrotoluene. The move follows an investigation by the EU, opened in September, into polyvinyl chloride imports from countries including China.

articles.title_orig: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage, disclosing state secrets and attempted treason
articles.title_zh: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage, disclosing state secrets and attempted treason
articles.content_orig:
Police have arrested the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency , August Hanning, on suspicion of espionage, the federal prosecutor's office announced Tuesday.
Hanning served as the agency's chief from December 1998 to November 2005 before moving to the Federal Interior Ministry, where he worked as state secretary until November 2009.
According to a statement from the prosecutor's office, the 80-year-old faces charges including espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason and working as a secret service agent.
It did not say which foreign intelligence service he is suspected of working for.
The statement added that another former high-ranking BND employee was also arrested on suspicion of providing hundreds of classified documents to Hanning after his tenure as spy chief ended in exchange for payment.
DW's chief political editor Michaela Küfner, reporting from a government press briefing on the arrest, described the case as Germany's "biggest espionage scandal of the century."
Police arrested Hanning early Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde near the western German city of Münster, according to information from WDR, NDR and the daily Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Hanning's alleged accomplice, who was identified only as Manfred D. in line with Germany's privacy laws, was taken into custody in Bavaria.
Authorities were conducting searches at both suspects' properties, as well as in Berlin, the prosecutor said.
During Hanning's tenure as spy head, D. served as his chief of staff. He also subsequently worked under Hanning at the Interior Ministry until 2009.
He is facing charges of "aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state."
Marc Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament's intelligence oversight committee, said following the arrests that Germany "will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets."
"Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out," he said in comments to the AFP news agency.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, also a member of the oversight committee, said the allegations were "deeply troubling" and called for a "swift and thorough investigation."
The investigation into Hanning reportedly began due to his connection to a high-profile trial involving businesswoman Christine Block.

The prosecutor's office said Hanning and Manfred D. are believed to have come up with their arrangement in 2010.
From 2012 to March 2026, D. served as chief of staff to Hanning's successors at the BND spy agency, where he had access to a wealth of classified documents, according to the prosecutor's statement.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement said.
It added that D. is alleged to have provided Hanning with information until at least mid-2022, and that Hanning used that information in his private consulting work.
"In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service," Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor's office, told German broadcaster RTL.
The prosecutor's statement said Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years."
Hanning and D. are expected to appear before an investigating judge on Tuesday and Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: XtalPi Debuts Kodexia™, the World's First Closed-Loop siRNA Platform Combining Generative AI with First-Principles Modeling
articles.content_orig:
BOSTON and BEIJING , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XtalPi Holdings Limited (HKEX: 2228), an AI and robotics-driven drug and materials discovery company, today debuted Kodexia™, the industry's first closed-loop small interfering RNA (siRNA) discovery platform combining generative AI, first-principles-driven biological modeling, and automated experimentation. Validating the rapid execution capabilities of this new infrastructure, the company simultaneously announced the advancement of six proprietary therapeutic programs, marking the successful expansion of XtalPi's technology into nucleic acid therapeutics.
By silencing disease-driving genes upstream of protein production, siRNA therapeutics offer immense potential for biological targets that conventional modalities struggle to address. However, clinical development remains heavily constrained by fragmented sequence and modification design processes, restrictive patent barriers, inconsistent translation from cellular assays to animal models, and severe limitations in extrahepatic delivery.
To address these interdependent bottlenecks, XtalPi drew on domain-specific expertise to develop siFormer, the proprietary architecture at the core of Kodexia™. By seamlessly integrating RNAi biological mechanisms with nucleic acid chemistry principles, siFormer delivers a qualitative leap in predictive accuracy that surpasses conventional design baselines. The architecture incorporates RNA thermodynamics and structural features relevant to strand loading, target accessibility, and silencing efficiency. These mechanistic constraints guide molecular generation toward biologically plausible designs rather than relying on sequence correlations alone. Through this unified approach, Kodexia™ enables researchers to systematically balance potency, in vivo translation, durability, off-target activity, safety, and patentability instead of optimizing single endpoints in isolation.
To execute this multiparameter optimization, XtalPi utilizes a closed-loop process of computational design, automated experimentation, and empirical feedback. Generative models and the proprietary siFormer architecture operate continuously with XtalPi's automated laboratories, which conduct more than 500 in vitro and 30 in vivo experiments weekly. This seamless integration enables the parallel development of multiple target programs, yielding a nearly threefold increase in design efficiency. Notably, more than 50% of first-round designs tested across multiple programs showed stronger in vivo activity than positive controls.
Kodexia™ also globally co-optimizes dual-target siRNAs as single molecules, creating a strategy for disease biology that may not be adequately addressed through single-target intervention. For extrahepatic delivery, the platform co-designs siRNA molecules with their targeting systems and applies multi-objective optimization to antibody, peptide, and small-molecule conjugates. These capabilities are being applied to delivery research targeting the kidney, spleen, and adipose tissue.
The platform's lead program in immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy serves as an early empirical validation of this unified architecture. The program reached non-human primate efficacy data within seven months, demonstrating greater activity and durability than a clinical-stage reference molecule targeting the same target. The program is on track for preclinical candidate selection within a nine-month project timeline, significantly accelerating the industry norm of 12 to 18 months.
Kodexia™ currently drives six proprietary programs across metabolic, renal, respiratory, and central nervous system diseases, with more than half having already completed in vivo efficacy evaluations. Each internal program generates high-value experimental data that feeds directly back into the platform's models, reinforcing a continuous cycle of discovery and commercial translation. As a global scientific utility platform, XtalPi leverages this capability alongside its established expertise in small molecules, antibodies, and peptides. By advancing these internal assets in tandem with established industry collaborations, XtalPi empowers its partners to pursue high-value targets using the modality best suited to the mechanistic and biophysical principles of RNA interference, including RNA thermodynamics and structural features, ultimately accelerating the delivery of next-generation RNA therapies for patients worldwide.
XtalPi Holdings Limited (XtalPi, 2228.HK) was founded in 2015 by three physicists from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). It is an innovative R&D platform powered by quantum physics, artificial intelligence, and robotics. By integrating first-principles calculations, AI algorithms, high-performance cloud computing, and standardized automation systems, XtalPi provides digital and intelligent R&D solutions for companies in the pharmaceutical, materials science, agricultural technology, energy, new chemicals, and cosmetics industries.

articles.title_zh: France Protests Live Updates: Unions Join Student Demonstrations
articles.content_orig:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 5,000 people have been taken into police custody, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.
Authorities estimate hundreds of thousands of protesters, including students, teachers and delegates from trade unions, took to the streets on Tuesday as protests sweep the country.
In Paris, tear gas filled the air, and trash cans, school desks and chairs were set alight as riot police with shields and batons clashed with some demonstrators.
The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.
“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”
Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.
The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.
A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.
Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).
There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”
The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.
France’s interior ministry estimated there were about 256,000 protesters out on the streets nationwide, including 56,000 in Paris. Meanwhile, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, one of the high school student unions involved in organizing the demonstrations, suggested a much larger turnout of 450,000 people across the country.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, said “extreme violence has reached the gates of our high schools and it must be condemned unequivocally.”
Lecornu said 215 students and 85 education staff have been injured during the unrest, calling it “the highest number of education staff injured in decades.” He rejected accusations that the government had ordered police to repress the protests.
The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.
The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.
Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”
The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.
CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne and Lucie Lepellec contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
“That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution, which is less than half a page, says.
The measure is expected to be considered by the faculty senate, which meets Oct. 14, according to a statement from faculty senator Paul Ortiz.
“The goal is to really force systemic change,” Ortiz, a professor of labor history, said in a statement.
Ortiz added that “students have been telling us stories they don’t feel safe, and this has been going on for a number of years” and called the situation a “systemic problem.” He reiterated that the senate was not “targeting any individual” but that the students and faculty “have been unsatisfied with the response.”
“Women need to feel safe,” he said.
In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty they were “upset, fearful for their personal safety,” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus.
Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement added.
Cornell declined to comment.
The proposed no-confidence resolution marks an escalation in pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with the alleged sexual assault.
She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana.
The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days and prompted protests on the university’s campus after widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate the woman’s allegations.
Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days.
“If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.”
Brady said that Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing on the case to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.”
“If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.”
If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty and Cornell’s leadership for policies affecting sexual assault.
Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady says those recommendations have largely been ignored.
“If the administration came out and said: ‘you know what? we screwed up, we did A, B, and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said. “If they did that? That goes so far.”
Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca; Matt Lavietes reported from New York City.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.title_zh: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom responded to the comments - made by Trump during a midterms rally in Nebraska - as  "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
While speaking in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, he said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was "disgusting and disqualifying".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 to
Francis Halzen University of Wisconsin–Madison, USA
“for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”
Francis Halzen realised that ice at the South Pole could be used to track particles known as neutrinos. His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors. Using IceCube, researchers can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe.
Neutrinos are everywhere, but they do not make themselves known. They pass all the way through the Earth and through our bodies without us noticing. Very rarely, a single neutrino will interact with an atomic nucleus, which makes it possible for someone with the right equipment to discover them.
Scientists have long known that the cosmos contains natural particle accelerators, which fire out particles with energies up to a million times more than can be achieved in laboratories on Earth. Much about these sources is mysterious: what are they, where are they, and what are the main processes inside them?
Neutrinos with extremely high energies are created in the same environments as other types of particles. However, unlike other particles, neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way.
Francis Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the clear glacial ice. The South Pole’s ice has many advantages, as it is free from various types of interference and the area is geologically stable, with no earthquakes. Halzen and his idea soon gained the support of other researchers and, just a few years later, preliminary testing was conducted on sensors in ice.
Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions. IceCube covers an entire cubic kilometre and was finished in 2011. Researchers soon discovered the first high-energy neutrinos and, a few years later, could publish their discovery of neutrinos that must originate far outside our solar system. The search for the universe’s neutrino sources could begin in earnest.
“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” says Mark Pearce, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.
The neutrino interactions that are continuously collected by IceCube will provide researchers with novel knowledge about the violent settings in which high-energy neutrinos can be created – and could even reveal previously unknown cosmic phenomena.

Artist Theo Triantafyllidis won this year’s Frieze Artist Award for his interactive sculpture, "Feral Metaverse (Spider)." This climbable, giant spider structure invites visitors to cooperate in both physical and digital gaming environments. You can see this collaborative project at Frieze London from October 14–18 or visit Google Arts & Culture to explore how the team used artificial intelligence to build it.
Artist Theo Triantafyllidis built a giant, climbable spider sculpture that doubles as a multiplayer video game. He worked with a huge team and used AI to help design the game’s look and digital world. Visitors have to help each other climb the spider to play, which encourages people to work together. It’s a cool way to show how art and technology can bring people closer.
Athens-based artist Theo Triantafyllidis is the recipient of this year’s Frieze Artist Award, which supports artists at pivotal moments in their careers as they create ambitious new work. Triantafyllidis works with video games, live simulations, performances, and physical installations to build playful worlds exploring complex phenomena. At Frieze London, he’ll present 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026,' a participatory climbable spider sculpture and live multiplayer game rooted in shared experiences.
In Triantafyllidis’ words, “spiders are the original engineers.” Strange, intelligent and unexpectedly tender, the spider became a central figure for an artwork built around physical contact, cooperation, and play.
Theo Triantafyllidis, Photo: Paris Tavitian, Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
From afar, the giant spider-shaped structure might appear intimidating, but up close, its softness invites touch. Visitors are encouraged to help one another climb the sculpture. Once players are aboard the legs, the experience extends into the Feral Metaverse, a shared digital environment where players collaborate, move, and form temporary collective bodies together.
Theo Triantafyllidis, 'Feral Metaverse (Spider), 2026.' Game still. Courtesy of the Artist and The Breeder, Athens.
The award allowed Triantafyllidis to expand his team of sculptors, fabricators, textile designers, game developers, and civil engineers. For this project, the group introduced Gemini into their workflow, working with it as a tool and collaborator as they generated the sketches, character designs, backdrops, and 3D renders that shaped the look and feel of the game. In rendering AI outputs as sculptural material, they were able to push both the game and the audience interaction with it.
The experience, which requires players to watch each other, exchange advice, and learn together, will move between the screen and the booth at Frieze. It’s a testament to how both public and online spaces can foster cooperation and warmth.

The S&P 500 rose to a fresh all-time intraday high on Tuesday, boosted by gains in key technology names as well as declines in oil prices and Treasury yields.
The broad market index was last up 0.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 205 points, or 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite added 0.5% and had hit a new all-time high as well.
The moves higher were bolstered by a rise in chipmakers. Shares of Marvell Technology popped 7%, while others such as Nvidia and Broadcom traded up around 1% each.
Additionally, the benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield fell 2 basis points to 5.29% after scaling to levels not seen since 2002 on Monday. The 2-year Treasury yield declined 3 basis points to 4.802%.
Bonds have been volatile over the past six weeks, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management investment chief Lisa Shalett said in a note to clients. She cited a potentially new Fed policy framework, economic growth and high oil prices while the Middle East conflict stretches on as factors.
"Nevertheless, while intraday implied volatility has risen, the six-week stretch has not reached the extremes that catalyzed the 2022 equity bear market," Shalett wrote.
Traders are now looking ahead to the Federal Reserve's minutes from its September meeting due Wednesday, which could shed some light on policymakers' move to raise rates.
Alongside Treasury yields, a drop in oil prices also gave equities a boost Tuesday. Brent crude traded 2% lower at around $98 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 1% to roughly $87 a barrel.

articles.title_orig: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.title_zh: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.content_orig:
By Jamie Durrani 2026-10-06T13:33:00+01:00
Source: © Nobel Prize Outreach/Niklas Elmehed
Francis Halzen is the first solo winner of the physics prize for more than 30 years
The 2026 Nobel prize in physics has been awarded to Belgian astrophysicist Francis Halzen for his work on the detection of high-energy cosmic neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy. Halzen spearheaded the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which has enabled scientists to track high-energy neutrinos that have reached Earth from the farthest reaches of the universe. It is the first time that the physics prize has been awarded to an individual recipient since 1992, when Georges Charpak was recognised for his work on particle detectors .
Neutrinos are elementary particles released by many different sources, including radioactive substances, the sun and other celestial bodies. But the neutrinos released by highly energetic processes like giant supernovae in the distant universe can have energies far higher than other cosmic neutrinos. As a result, these high-energy neutrinos – which have no charge and almost no mass – travel across the universe barely interacting with other matter and without changing direction or losing energy. This means that when these neutrinos reach the Earth they carry information about extreme environments in distant regions of space that cannot be gathered by monitoring other types of radiation such as light or gamma rays.
But the very properties that make high-energy cosmic neutrinos such useful carriers of information also make them incredibly difficult to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen came up with the idea of building a giant facility at the South Pole, where flashes of blue light given off as neutrinos pass through the Antarctic ice could be tracked. Halzen and his colleague John Learned presented the concept at a conference in Poland in June 1988.
Source: © Johan Jamestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
The IceCube neutrino observatory is a huge cubic kilometre of ice dotted with sensors that was the brainchild of Halzen
Since then, Halzen, who works at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, has spent years developing techniques to detect neutrinos, contributing to projects in Greenland and Antarctica that honed the technology. Eventually, he led an initiative that culminated in the construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, in which more than 5000 special sensors are spread across a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice deep below the surface.
The IceCube facility was completed in 2011, and uncovered the first evidence of high-energy cosmic neutrinos just two years later. The project involves more than 450 researchers from 14 countries and has paved the way for further international collaboration to detect cosmic neutrinos. Speaking at the prize announcement, the Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce noted that a global network of neutrino telescopes, based in ice and the oceans, is currently being established, which will allow researchers to ‘monitor all of the sky, all of the time’.
Speaking on the phone immediately after the announcement, Halzen described the award as ‘a great surprise’ and emphasised the critical contributions from his collaborators over the years. ‘When we started this project, everybody realised this was a good idea, but very few thought it would work – including myself,’ he said. ‘So this was an adventure where success was not guaranteed and we were lucky to overcome the various challenges, partly because the talent of collaborators and partly because of luck. It was a long journey, but it finally worked.’

Officials file ‘denaturalization actions’ against people accused of crimes in what they call ‘largest’ such initiative
Donald Trump ’s justice department has moved to strip the citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in what authorities describe as “the largest” such initiative over a single period during his administration.
US justice department officials on Monday announced the filing of “denaturalization actions” against more than three dozen people alleged to have committed such offenses as “acting as an agent for a foreign government, committing voluntary manslaughter, and aggravated sodomy against a special‑needs man”.
The denaturalization requests in question were submitted in multiple federal courts between 21 August and 2 October, according to the justice department.
The federal Immigration and Nationality Act allows for naturalized US citizenship to be revoked by a federal court if the government proves that it was illegally obtained through concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation.
A statement attributed to the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, maintained those at the center of Monday’s announcement “concealed critical facts from the US government and represent serious criminal offenders”.
Trump in previous months had reportedly pushed the US justice department to pursue denaturalization cases en masse. The New York Times reported in April that the justice department had identified at least 384 foreign-born US citizens whose naturalization it wanted to revoke.
Denaturalization requests to courts often involve individuals who lied to government authorities during the naturalization process or obtained citizenship through false marriages. There are also some instances where people who committed criminal offenses can lose their citizenship.
In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second presidency, the justice department filed a memo instructing its civil division to ramp up denaturalization efforts, including by adopting more categories of individuals qualifying for denaturalization – which experts have said has supported the president’s mass deportation agenda .
Because denaturalization cases are costly and require extensive manpower, the justice department has historically pursued them only sporadically.
From 2017 to late 2025, the US denaturalized about 120 people, the Times reported. A justice department official said the initiative reported by the Times in April marked only “the first wave” of citizenship-stripping cases.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, the Department of Justice will continue to employ the denaturalization process to maintain our national security and protect the American people,” Blanche’s statement on Monday said.
The 40 people subject to denaturalization proceedings announced on Monday came from various countries, among them Mexico, China, Iran, Pakistan and the Philippines.
One of those individuals was Jinchao Wei , a former Chinese-born US navy sailor who was convicted in August 2025 of charges including espionage and unlawfully exporting technical data related to defense articles. Prosecutors have said Wei began plotting to sell military secrets to China months before becoming a US citizen in May 2022 and concealed that conduct during the naturalization process.
Wei was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison.

A new Radio World ebook considers trends in consoles and control surfaces. In this companion piece, Mark Ruddy takes our questions. He’s chief engineer at WVIA Public Media , covering Northeast and Central Pennsylvania.
Radio World: Mark, what do you consider the most important trend in the design of consoles and control surfaces for radio broadcast studios?
Mark Ruddy: It seems that consoles are trending as less of a hardware item, and more of a software item.
The shift to an on-screen console seems that it can work for some applications, but I am happy to see that innovations continue in hardware-based control surfaces. Being a radio station that operates with live personnel, they are familiar with the layout of a hardware-based console. The most important functions for me as an engineer are to see levels for a source that is loaded into a channel and for the surface to function reliably and accurately.
Even though control surfaces are trending smaller, it is good that options still remain for larger layouts and designs.
RW: What is the definition of a radio console now?
Ruddy: In most cases, it is akin to a keyboard for a computer. It is there and functions as a radio console, but really with other means to connect, it is less critical of a component for operation. The exception does exist still for analog or digital-based consoles, but when audio isn’t passing directly though the console, it’s more of an interface.
RW: How has their evolution changed the way engineers view them and plan around their installation?
Ruddy: The evolution of consoles into control surfaces has certainly made things more efficient and effective when planning installation. In most cases it is just running a network cable and power, with the audio entering the system through other means, the installation of a control surface is much neater and in the case of AoIP, it keeps wiring localized and minimizes cable runs.
RW: To what extent has scripting changed console operations, and what does scripting make possible?
Ruddy: Scripting allows for more under-the-hood tasks to be accomplished without anybody realizing what it is doing. Even by doing simple routes or logic controls, it’s very much more efficient.
If you have an automation system that integrates with your installation, it makes things even easier for an operator by being able to execute a hotkey and not having to worry about anything else.
RW: How vibrant is the marketplace for analog consoles?
Ruddy: I believe that there is still a need for analog consoles and will be. Some stations don’t need much more than that for their operations, and they are very useful for at-home studios. Current analog consoles make for a cost-effective upgrade for an aging console.
RW: Any suggested best practices or common errors to avoid when choosing one?
Ruddy: Just recognize your requirements, then make sure to research all available options. What is right for one operation isn’t necessarily right for another. There are many manufacturers making quality consoles and systems, but each one does have its pros and cons. I would also say to reach out to other stations or groups who are using the system you’re looking at to get their opinion and run questions by them as well. That was invaluable for me in choosing our current system.

articles.title_zh: New York governor declares state of emergency after spike in measles cases
articles.content_orig:
The deadly outbreak in Pennsylvania is its largest in more than three decades, and confirmed cases in New York are up
The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency on Monday in response to a dramatic spike in measles cases in the state.
Hochul’s administration said the emergency declaration was in response to a “growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states”, including Pennsylvania , which has been grappling with a deadly outbreak that is its largest in more than three decades.
The declaration expands the pool of people who can administer vaccines against measles and allows more individuals to order testing.
It comes as there have been 108 confirmed cases of measles in New York so far for the year, up from just one reported case in 2023. In Pennsylvania, which neighbors New York, five people have died after contracting the disease, and there have been 198 hospitalizations.
The state surpassed 1,000 measles cases on Monday while Ohio has also seen an increase.
New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio have sizable Amish populations, which tend to be undervaccinated. And undervaccination has been a driving factor in measles spreading after its domestic US spread had been eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates.
“After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York state, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.”
The US is experiencing its worst year for measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with nearly 3,900 cases reported.
Of New York’s 108 measles cases, 101 have been reported outside of New York City, the state said. Since 15 July, 92 cases have been reported in underimmunized rural communities.
It is a stark increase from previous years. Beside the one reported case in 2023, there were only 15 in 2024 – and in 2025, there were a total of 48 measles cases.
The Trump administration health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr , has been criticized for his response to the measles outbreak. Before his appointment as health secretary, he was best known as an anti-vaccine activist.
Kennedy headlined an anti-vaccine conference in Washington DC in mid-September, as measles cases surged. He told the crowd there that they had a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House”.
Meanwhile, the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and the two men have clashed over how to classify measles-related deaths.
“The concerning rise in measles cases is due to a decrease in childhood vaccines driven by misinformation and is causing a public health emergency,” said state senator Gustavo Rivera, who chairs the senate’s health committee.
At least 95% of a community must be vaccinated against measles to prevent outbreaks.

articles.title_orig: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
articles.title_zh: Goodbye joint replacements? Stanford scientists found a way to regrow cartilage and stop arthritis
articles.content_orig:
Scientists have identified a way to restore cartilage in aging knee joints, at least in mice, by blocking a protein whose levels rise with age. The approach not only reversed naturally occurring cartilage loss in older animals, but also protected mice from developing arthritis after knee injuries similar to ACL tears in people.
The findings also showed promise in human tissue. Cartilage samples collected during knee replacement surgeries responded to the treatment by beginning to produce new, functional cartilage.
Together, the results suggest that cartilage damaged by aging or arthritis may be more capable of repair than previously thought. If the strategy ultimately works in people, researchers believe it could potentially lead to an oral medicine or injection that regenerates cartilage and reduces the need for knee or hip replacement surgery.
Targeting the damage behind osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease in which cartilage gradually breaks down, leaving joints painful, swollen and increasingly difficult to move. It affects about one in five adults in the United States and is estimated to account for roughly $65 billion in direct health care costs each year.
Current treatments mainly focus on controlling pain and other symptoms. Once the disease becomes severe, replacing the damaged joint surgically may be the only remaining option. There is currently no drug that can reliably slow or reverse osteoarthritis itself.
The Stanford Medicine-led study instead focused on a protein called 15-PGDH. The researchers have described it as a gerozyme, a term for enzymes that become more abundant with age and contribute to the gradual loss of tissue function.
Previous work by the same group showed that 15-PGDH acts as an important regulator of aging in multiple tissues. Blocking the protein with a small molecule increased muscle mass and endurance in old mice. Doing the opposite, increasing 15-PGDH in young animals, caused their muscles to shrink and weaken. The protein has also been linked to the regeneration of bone, nerve and blood cells.
In many of those tissues, healing depends on tissue-specific stem cells multiplying and developing into specialized cells. Cartilage turned out to behave differently. Instead of relying on stem cells, existing cartilage cells called chondrocytes changed their patterns of gene activity and shifted toward a more youthful state.
"This is a new way of regenerating adult tissue, and it has significant clinical promise for treating arthritis due to aging or injury," said Helen Blau, PhD, professor of microbiology and immunology. "We were looking for stem cells, but they are clearly not involved. It's very exciting."
Blau, who directs the Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology and is the Donald E. and Delia B. Baxter Foundation Professor, and Nidhi Bhutani, PhD, associate professor of orthopaedic surgery, are the senior authors of the research, which was published in Science . Instructor of orthopedic surgery Mamta Singla, PhD, and former postdoctoral scholar Yu Xin (Will) Wang, PhD, are the lead authors of the study. Wang is now an assistant professor at the Sanford Burnham Institute in San Diego.
"Dramatic regeneration" of cartilage
"Millions of people suffer from joint pain and swelling as they age," Bhutani said. "It is a huge unmet medical need. Until now, there has been no drug that directly treats the cause of cartilage loss. But this gerozyme inhibitor causes a dramatic regeneration of cartilage beyond that reported in response to any other drug or intervention."
Cartilage is not all the same. The human body contains three major types, each designed for a different job.
Elastic cartilage is soft and flexible and helps form structures such as the outer ear. Fibrocartilage is tougher and better suited to absorbing force, including in areas between the vertebrae of the spine. Hyaline cartilage is smooth and slippery, allowing bones to move against one another with very little friction in joints such as the ankles, hips, shoulders and parts of the knee.
In joints, hyaline cartilage is also known as articular cartilage. It is the type most commonly damaged by osteoarthritis.
Osteoarthritis can develop as joints experience stress from aging, injury or obesity. Chondrocytes begin producing inflammatory molecules while also breaking down collagen, a structural protein that gives cartilage much of its strength.
As collagen disappears, cartilage becomes thinner and softer. Inflammation adds swelling and pain, creating the familiar symptoms of osteoarthritis.
The problem is that articular cartilage normally has very little ability to repair itself. Researchers have identified possible stem or progenitor cells capable of forming cartilage in bone, but efforts to find similar cell populations within articular cartilage itself have not been successful.
An aging protein becomes a target
Earlier research from Blau's laboratory found that a molecule called prostaglandin E2 is important for the function of muscle stem cells. The protein 15-PGDH breaks down prostaglandin E2.
Blocking 15-PGDH, or otherwise raising levels of prostaglandin E2, has been shown to support regeneration in damaged muscle, nerve, bone, colon, liver and blood cells in young mice.
That raised an important question for Blau, Bhutani and their colleagues: Could the same biological pathway contribute to the deterioration of cartilage as animals age or recover from injury?
The researchers compared 15-PGDH levels in knee cartilage from young and old mice. They found that the amount of the gerozyme roughly doubled with age.
They then gave older animals a small molecule drug designed to inhibit 15-PGDH. In one experiment, the drug was injected into the abdomen so it could have effects throughout the body. In another, it was delivered directly into the knee joint.
Both approaches produced striking results.
Cartilage in the knees of older animals had been noticeably thinner and less functional than cartilage in young mice. After treatment, however, it became thicker across the surface of the joint.
Importantly, the cells were making hyaline cartilage, the smooth articular cartilage needed for healthy joint movement, rather than the less suitable fibrocartilage.
"Cartilage regeneration to such an extent in aged mice took us by surprise," Bhutani said. "The effect was remarkable."
Protecting knees after ACL injuries
The researchers also tested whether the treatment could help after traumatic knee injuries.
ACL tears are particularly common in sports such as soccer, basketball and skiing, where athletes frequently pivot, stop abruptly or jump. Surgery can repair the torn ligament, but fixing the immediate injury does not necessarily prevent long-term joint damage.
About 50% of people who experience these injuries go on to develop osteoarthritis in the affected joint within approximately 15 years.
In the mouse experiments, researchers administered the gerozyme inhibitor twice a week for four weeks after injury. The treatment dramatically reduced the likelihood that the animals would develop osteoarthritis.
Mice that received a control drug had 15-PGDH levels twice those of animals whose knees had not been injured, and they developed osteoarthritis within four weeks.
The treated mice also moved more normally and placed more weight on the paw attached to the injured leg than untreated animals did.
"Interestingly, prostaglandin E2 has been implicated in inflammation and pain," Blau said. "But this research shows that, at normal biological levels, small increases in prostaglandin E2 can promote regeneration."
Making old cartilage cells act younger
To understand what was happening inside the joint, the researchers took a closer look at chondrocytes from young and old mice.

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow student of Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”
