articles.title_orig: Hidden Beauty: UVM student explores Lake Champlain’s underwater world
articles.title_zh: Hidden Beauty: UVM student explores Lake Champlain’s underwater world
articles.content_orig:
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
Graham Montague, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Vermont, is diving into Lake Champlain to showcase its underwater wonders and sharing his discoveries with thousands of followers online.
"I started doing just for a creative outlet and just to make videos that I wanted to actually see myself," Montague said. "I do this all the time anyways, but I started taking my GoPro with me and just started filming fish underneath the water just for fun."
Since 2023, Montague has been documenting life beneath the surface, highlighting underwater vegetation, shipwrecks, and various fish species. His passion for aquatic exploration began with a backyard stream at the Cuyahoga Valley National Park in northeastern Ohio.
"There's so much cool things to see underneath water, but if you're not actually in the water, you're not going to be able to see them," Montague said. "To highlight the beauty of the underwater species is super fun. And it also just gets me outside."
Montague’s academic work focuses on natural resources, aquatic ecology, and fisheries. His current research at UVM examines Lake Champlain’s distinct basins, each with unique environments and fish populations, and tracks how stocked Atlantic salmon move between them.
"We've been tracking them for a couple of years now, and we're finding that Atlantic salmon are moving very far distances throughout the lake and even potentially out of the lake, which is super cool," Montague said.
Between his research and social media videos, Montague hopes to inspire others to explore and protect nature, whether in their own backyard or beneath the surface of a lake.
"The backyard stream in your backyard is going to have a lot of cool fish and wildlife too. That also needs to be conserved and protected and love," Montague said. "So just get outside, enjoy nature, and really just follow what you're passionate about."
Montague’s work demonstrates that you don’t have to look far, or stay above the surface to find something worth protecting.

As an ongoing Diamond Partner of WSAVA, Purina Institute will support the congress through its sponsored "Food for Thought" educational stream including eight globally renowned speakers, and as the sole sponsor of the WSAVA Global State of Companion Animal Veterinary Practice Report 2026, which will launch during the event.

"The WSAVA World Congress offers an important opportunity to listen, learn and share science that can make a difference in everyday veterinary practice," said Dr Marianne Lomberg, Head of Purina Institute. "Through our ongoing partnership with WSAVA, we are helping make nutrition knowledge more accessible and actionable so veterinary teams can support healthier, longer lives for pets."
Beyond the congress, Purina Institute supports several WSAVA committees and initiatives that help veterinary teams apply science in practice. This includes contributing to work with the Nutrition, Education, Animal Welfare and Wellness Committees, as well as work related to One Health and Therapeutics Committees. The Purina Institute also supports strategic WSAVA initiatives through regional Continuing Education events, the annual webinar series and the WSAVA Nutrition Guidelines Course.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title_orig: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.title_zh: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.content_orig:
From the latest big breakthrough to the most influential and inspiring figures on campus to Pitt in the community, Pittwire is your official source for what’s happening now.
Kati Csoman was still an undergraduate at the University of Pittsburgh when she lived in Hungary for the first time.
She spent the summer of 1988 in the rural northeastern village where her father had grown up. She slept in cousins’ homes, some of which didn’t have indoor plumbing. She picked up Hungarian with a village accent and, for the first time in her life, the language she heard at her childhood kitchen table became something she could speak back.
The immersion into this experience came courtesy of a Nationality Rooms scholarship .
“It really helped me to connect to that part of my life, which is so deeply a part of me,” she says. Three years later, she arrived back in Budapest on a state department fellowship to the U.S. embassy, watching firsthand how Hungary would remake itself after her father’s country voted in its first free elections since the 1940s.
“But, also, it totally changed my academic trajectory and then changed my professional trajectory, too.”
The scholarship launched Csoman (A&S ’89, SPIA ’96G) on a career in international education and connected her not only to her family’s history but also to a broader appreciation of ethnic communities and cross-cultural experiences.
And, eventually, it would lead her back to where it all began.
Today, Csoman is director of Pitt’s Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs, home to 31 spaces inside the Cathedral of Learning that represent the cultural heritages of many of Pittsburgh’s international communities.
The rooms were first imagined in the mid-1920s by Chancellor John Bowman, who wanted a celebration of Pittsburgh’s multicultural presence at the heart of his planned Cathedral of Learning . He turned to Ruth Crawford Mitchell, a Pitt sociologist already closely associated with the city’s ethnic communities through her work with second-generation immigrant students. She gave the program its shape at a time when nearly half of Pittsburgh residents were either born abroad or the children of immigrants. Communities could sponsor classrooms in the Cathedral and, once room construction was complete, leftover funds supported scholarships to send Pitt students abroad year after year. [Watch: Pitt's Nationality and Heritage Rooms are also celebrating a centennial this year. ]
Mitchell stepped back from the directorship in 1957. Shepherd Witman, who arrived at Pitt the following year to direct the Office of Cultural and Educational Exchange, oversaw the rooms during a transitional period, while E. Maxine Bruhns would take the reins in 1965. Bruhns led the Nationality Rooms for the next 55 years, when 12 of the 31 rooms were dedicated and scholarship programs were expanded significantly. Bruhns retired in 2020, with Csoman succeeding her the following year.
But the rooms touched Csoman’s own family long before. Her maternal grandfather had given a dime to help build the Cathedral. Csoman’s father later served on the Hungarian Room Committee, and Csoman herself volunteered with it before becoming the program’s director.
Since the late 1940s, the Nationality Rooms program has supported more than 1,800 Pitt undergrads or graduate students with study abroad scholarships, awarding nearly $5 million in funding. Thirty committees, plus the Women’s International Club, still meet; they fundraise and produce intercultural programming for the campus and wider community, and nearly all of the rooms presently serve as active classrooms or gathering places.
From conceptualization to fundraising to dedication, Pittsburgh’s international communities have shaped each of the rooms into a cultural self-portrait. Every room is designed with precise choices about what best represents a community and how it wants to be seen. A century in, the following stories, centered on the Chinese (dedicated 1939) , Italian (1949) , African Heritage (1989) and Philippine (2019) rooms, reveal examples of how these spaces bridge past and present and often reshape a life’s trajectory.
The Chinese community was not on Mitchell’s original list. In her earliest report to Bowman, Mitchell named 14 ethnic groups interested in building rooms; most were Eastern, Central or Southern European.
While the Chinese community was kept small in the United States by the Immigration Act of 1924 and other federal policies, a group of Chinese graduate students at Pitt sought out Bowman anyway. The Chancellor told them that if they could fundraise and form a committee, they could have a room, says Michael Walter, current manager of education programs for the Nationality Rooms. They organized quickly.
City-wide development also had a significant impact on Pittsburgh’s Chinese community at that time.
The city’s Chinatown neighborhood spanned multiple blocks downtown, but ended up physically divided in the 1920s and 1930s by construction of the city’s Boulevard of the Allies. Pittsburgh’s Chinatown district was all but gone in the following decades with residents moving outward.
Still, the Chinese Room became one of the first nine rooms at Pitt to reach completion. The German, Russian, Scottish, Swedish and Early American rooms were dedicated in 1938, while the Chinese, Czechoslovak, Hungarian and Yugoslav rooms came next in 1939.
The Chinese Room was modeled on an 18th-century reception hall in Beijing’s Forbidden City, the imperial palace at the heart of Ming and Qing dynasty rule.
This art installation inside Hillman Library examines a century of Nationality Rooms history. The installation will run through July 2027.
Yuefang Chang, a research associate professor in Pitt’s School of Medicine’s Department of Neurological Surgery, has been involved with the room for more than a decade, chairing the Chinese Room Committee for the past year and a half.
Chang has worked to learn the room’s history herself, noting that “even within the Chinese community, if they didn’t get a chance to go to the University, they just don’t know about its existence here.”
The first time Chang walked into the room, it surprised her. She had expected the colors to look brighter; instead, the dragons and phoenixes had softened over the decades.
But age and history are essential parts of the experience. Each Nationality Room’s design draws on cultural and traditional markers from before 1787 — the year of Pitt’s founding — meaning every room depicts something far older than the present. Decades of classes, holiday open houses and committee gatherings have only deepened that. Time is the point.
The Chinese Room is full of imperial signifiers: a five-clawed dragon on the ceiling (only the imperial dragon has five, a marker of leadership), phoenixes among peony blossoms, Confucius on the east wall and a round table at the center.
Chang’s committee today includes connections to Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia and the broader diaspora. This year, the Chinese Room committee and the John H. Tsui Memorial Scholarship, named for and seeded by a former chair, together will send seven students to China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
“We all have different backgrounds,” Chang says. “I just hope this room will bring everybody together.”
On the steps of Florence’s Basilica of Santa Maria Novella, Lina Insana (A&S ’91, ’95G) sits with her students and reads from Giovanni Boccaccio’s “The Decameron,” which opens with 10 young Florentines gathered on those same steps in 1348, fleeing the Black Death.
“It was a wonderful way to read that together in a classroom that wasn’t a classroom at all,” she says. Insana, an associate professor of Italian in the Kenneth P. articles.title_orig: The climate crisis will not wait for the world’s geopolitics to improve
articles.title_zh: The climate crisis will not wait for the world’s geopolitics to improve
articles.content_orig:
In our latest newsletter, Gro Harlem Brundtland looks ahead to COP31 in Turkey and calls for world leaders to act courageously to tackle climate change.
The climate crisis will not wait for the world’s geopolitics to improve. As leaders gather for COP31 in Turkey next month, half-measures are no longer enough. They must arrive with the courage to act, not just statements to describe the situation. And they must leave Antalya with commitments equal to the scale of the crises we are already experiencing: record heatwaves, devastating floods, and a major energy-security shock created by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The pressures are only mounting. A Super El Niño – exacerbated by climate change - now threatens to increase the risks of drought, extreme heat, floods and storms across the globe. The additional heat alone is projected to cause 450,000 more deaths worldwide. As world leaders prepare for COP31 in Turkey next month, they must have the tenacity and vision to work together to tackle the challenge head on. There must be clear leadership from the COP Presidencies of Australia and Turkey. They must mobilise countries behind a clear and credible plan for tangible progress. As Elders, we are clear on the direction of travel: this is the moment to accelerate the just transition away from fossil fuels and towards clean energy, decisively.
The answer to the twin challenges we face – extreme weather and energy security – cannot be to double down on the energy sources that have left us exposed. Instead, we must accelerate the global transition to secure, affordable and clean energy. France and Germany have set the ball rolling – both publishing national roadmaps with timelines for phasing out the use of coal, oil and gas. We must see more countries following in their footsteps. Throughout my career in public service, I have argued that the way to secure our common future is through solidarity and collective action. These principles are more vital now than ever. Promisingly, we have seen two coalitions emerge over the course of this year: the Santa Marta initiative, focused on accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels, and Electrify Now, focused on expanding electrification. COP31 offers a key moment to build on this good momentum and for countries, cities and companies to find fresh opportunities for collaboration.
Another area where more progress needs to be made is that of climate finance, which moves far slower than the pace of the climate crisis. It is often those who have contributed the least to global emissions that are now suffering the most. As the world tips over the 1.5 degrees threshold, no community should be left to face a climate disaster without adequate protection.
Those who have had the greatest hand in causing the climate crisis must not shirk their responsibilities. Developed countries must lead in delivering the promised climate finance to help people adapt and respond to climate extremes.
I hope that Turkey and Australia can rally countries at COP31 to respond with greater action and practical partnerships. As extreme weather events and high energy prices are set to continue, the world will be watching.
With thanks for your ongoing support, Gro Harlem Brundtland

A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.title_zh: Pumpkin named Bagheera breaks world record for Lymington grower
articles.content_orig:
A pumpkin grower has set a new world record after producing a giant squash.
Ian Paton, from Lymington, Hampshire, entered his exceptionally large specimen into a giant vegetable weigh-off near Reading in Berkshire.
It weighed 2,856.8lbs (1,295.8kg), has circumference of over 20ft (6m) and was officially confirmed by Guinness World Records judge, Sebastian Suski.
Paton said growing the pumpkin named Bagheera, tending to it for up to six hours and providing about 130 gallons of water daily, had been "bloody hard work". It was the first time the 65-year-old, who has grown giant pumpkins with his twin brother Stuart for over 50 years, had entered the competition on his own.
The pumpkin is now on show at Sunnyfields farm near Southampton, where it will be displayed for the next few weeks.
The farm has used more than 10,000 pumpkins and squashes to create a giant pumpkin mural of Sir David Attenborough .
Paton said the pumpkin would later be used as feed for cows.

articles.title_orig: Jannik Sinner Ends 2026 Season For Knee Recovery, Alexander Zverev Set To Become World No. 1
articles.title_zh: Jannik Sinner Ends 2026 Season For Knee Recovery, Alexander Zverev Set To Become World No. 1
articles.content_orig:
World number one men’s tennis player Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.
The five-time Grand Slam winner will “follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee”, Sinner’s team said in a statement on Tuesday.
“The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027. As a result, Jannik will be unable to compete again during the 2026 season.”
Sinner also posted the update on his personal Instagram account, where he recounted ending last year on a high after retaining his ATP Finals title in Turin as he battled past then world number one Carlos Alcaraz.
“But at the moment, I also need to think about my long-term career,” he said in a video posted on Instagram.
“I will do everything possible to get back to 100 percent [and] I hope to see you very, very soon on court again.”
Sinner, 25, has not played since his triumph at the All England ⁠⁠Club, missing the North American hardcourt swing, including the US Open , and the ongoing ATP 500 event in Beijing.
He announced last week that he was withdrawing from the Shanghai Masters , which he won in 2024 after defeating Novak Djokovic in the final.
Now he will also miss the Paris Masters and the ATP Finals in November. Plus, he will not be able to play for Italy, the host nation and three-time defending champion, in the Davis Cup Final 8.
Sinner risks losing the top ranking while he’s out.
But if Sinner does return at the start of next year, he could play the Australian Open – the next Grand Slam – which starts January 17.
He enjoyed a 30-match winning streak this year before his meltdown in a second-round defeat at the French Open amid a Paris heatwave.
Sinner’s main rival missed four and a half months this year due to a right wrist injury.
Meanwhile, Germany’s Alexander Zverev won two of the four Grand Slam titles and is nearing the No 1 ranking.

articles.title_orig: Jim Bakker, disgraced televangelist who went to prison, dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jim Bakker, disgraced televangelist who went to prison, dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
In the halcyon days of the televangelists, when Jim Bakker stood shoulder to shoulder with fire and brimstone preachers such as Jerry Farwell, Pat Robertson and Jimmy Swaggart, the collection plate always seemed bottomless.
For Bakker, it meant a Christian theme park in a leafy Charlotte, N.C., suburb, a fleet of black Cadillac limousines, vacation homes, regular orders of truffles flown in from Brussels, a gold-plated bathtub, mink coats for his wife Tammy Faye and an air-conditioned doghouse at the family compound.
In return for your unbending faith, he told viewers of his popular television show “The PTL Club,” God will bestow you great wealth and other blessings. And to get things rolling, he added, just call the 800 number on the bottom of your screen.
By the time it all fell apart amid a sex scandal and a fraud conviction, Bakker landed in prison and took stock of his life. He renounced the prosperity gospel he once had preached, wrote a raw and wrenching biography about his missteps and vowed to work with the needy and most vulnerable when he was released.
Once free, however, he set up camp at a Christian compound deep in the Ozarks, armed with a darker message. The End Times are upon us, he told viewers on his reborn television show, and the signs are everywhere — terrorist attacks, epic storms, thunderous earthquakes, frayed relations among world superpowers, a pandemic that refused to release its grip.
To get viewers to the Rapture he said was sure to come, Bakker sold buckets of freeze-dried food with a shelf life of 30 years, fuel-less generators, doomsday guides and a magical elixir — “Silver Solution” — that could cure the coronavirus and other unpleasantries. “Imagine — the world is dying and you’re having breakfast like a king,” he told viewers.
And, as before, the authorities were hot on his tail.
A man of confounding contradictions, Bakker died Monday, his wife announced in a statement on his Instagram account. He was 86.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” read the statement from Bakker’s wife, Lori Bakker. “Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years.”
Baby-faced with dark lacquered hair and oversized glasses, Bakker became the sunny alternative to the hell-fire bombast of Swaggart and Falwell when he and his wife introduced themselves to America when “The PTL Club” debuted in 1976.
The show, an acronym for Praise the Lord, was breezy and chatty, styled after a late-night talk show with a lineup of guests, performances by Christian musicians and the never-a-mean-word banter between Bakker and Tammy Faye, who would frequently burst into song, tears dribbling down her cheeks.
Together the Bakkers spoke of the souls saved and the hardships overcome by those who put their lives in the hands of the Lord. And as often, reminded viewers of the need for donations to keep their crusade barreling forward. Before long, according to evidence introduced at Bakker’s fraud trial, more than $1 million a week was pouring into “The PTL Club.”
Capitalizing on their fame and fortune, the Bakkers opened Heritage USA, a Christian theme park complete with a $12-million water park, a hotel, nightly Passion plays and a Disneyesque Main Street where guests could buy palm-size Jesus dolls, 24-carat gold crosses and boxes of Heavenly Fudge. As the guests rolled in, developers built condos and homes for those who wished to live in such a place.
Tammy Faye Messner, the mascara-laden former wife of televangelist Jim Bakker, the charismatic TV preacher with the choir-boy face with whom she appeared on their popular Christian talk-variety show until his downfall amid scandal in the late 1980s, has died.
It was all heady stuff for Bakker, who often said that as a youth he had few expectations. Born Jan. 2, 1940, James Orsen Bakker was raised in Muskegon, a commercial ship port in Michigan just across the lake from Milwaukee. He said his parents were deeply religious and so strict that even simple pleasures such as singing were forbidden.
At North Central University, a Minneapolis Bible college affiliated with the Assemblies of God, he met Tammy Faye LaValley. They married four months later, dropped out school and launched their television evangelism careers as hosts of a children’s puppet show on Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network. They eventually set off on their own to develop a show that paired church and pop culture, “The PTL Club.”
By the mid-1980s, “The PTL Club” had a daily viewership of roughly 5.7 million and more than 6 million visitors a year were rolling into Heritage USA. But it would all quickly vaporize.
It started with a rendezvous in a hotel room in Clearwater Beach, Fla., where Bakker met up with church secretary Jessica Hahn, a sexual encounter he successfully kept under wraps for years by reportedly paying her hush money. But when Swaggart caught wind of the tryst, he saw an opportunity to topple his rival and took the matter to the Assemblies of God, the church fellowship both preachers belonged to.
Accused of “moral failure” by the fellowship, Bakker resigned and Falwell replaced him as president of PTL. Once there, Falwell examined the company ledgers and realized he had a problem. Among other things, Bakker had offered nearly 160,000 people the opportunity to reserve a room at the 500-room Heritage Grand Hotel for three nights a year for life for $1,000 — a mathematical impossibility.
Bakker was eventually sentenced to 45 years in prison and fined $500,000 after jurors found him guilty on 24 fraud and conspiracy charges, which accused him of swindling his followers out of nearly $160 million and using much of it to fund his extravagance lifestyle. His sentence was later cut to eight years.
“Please don’t do this to me,” Bakker said before he was led away in handcuffs.
His attorney told The Times after his client was sentenced that Bakker had suffered a nervous breakdown during the trial and was overcome by vivid hallucinations, imaging that those packed in the courtroom were “frightening animals intent on destroying him.”
Behind bars, Bakker learned that Tammy Faye had filed for divorce, a final blow that left him questioning his faith, he later told Larry King. Ultimately, though, he said he “learned more in prison than in Bible college” and read the Bible in full for the first time, coming to realize that he had been leading “an ungodly arrogant lifestyle” as he chased wealth.
“You can worship money or you can worship God,” he told The Times when he moved into a small apartment in Burbank with his son after his release. “But you can’t worship both.”
The apartment served as a base camp after he released his memoir, “I Was Wrong,” and plotted a national book tour. He also did volunteer work at the Los Angeles International Dream Center, where he was welcomed warmly by the poor families and troubled youths who sought a fresh start there.
Tammy Faye Bakker says Jessica Hahn “knew exactly what she was doing” when she traveled to Florida in 1980 for the fateful meeting with Jim Bakker that eventually led to the PTL scandal.
It’s also where he met Lori Beth Graham, an evangelist and frequent speaker at the center who described herself as a survivor of an abusive marriage and a hard-partying lifestyle as a youth. Both were broke, and she told the Charlotte Observer she had to borrow a wedding gown when they married in 1988.
The newlyweds moved to rural Missouri, just north of the Arkansas boarder, and set up camp on 800 rolling acres that had been purchased by developer Jerry Crawford, a onetime PTL partner who credited Bakker with saving his failing marriage. Bakker

articles.title_orig: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.title_zh: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX now owns every spot on the list of the five fastest trips a U.S. spacecraft has ever made to the International Space Station, and its newest entry beat the old mark by more than four hours.
Crew Dragon Grace docked to the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at 7:05 p.m. ET on October 1, just 7 hours and 55 minutes after lifting off from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral. NASA confirmed the milestone in a space station blog update , writing that the flight “marked the fastest launch‑to‑docking of a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the International Space Station.”
The previous U.S. record also belonged to Dragon. SpaceX’s uncrewed CRS-31 cargo mission reached the station in a little over 12 hours in November 2024. The fastest crewed trip before last week was Crew-11, which took 14 hours and 43 minutes in August 2025, according to Space.com .
A post that Elon Musk reposted on Monday filled out the rest of the ranking. Behind Crew-13, CRS-31 and Crew-11 sit Axiom’s Ax-2 mission at 15 hours and 35 minutes and NASA’s Crew-4 at 15 hours and 44 minutes. All five flew on Dragon.
SpaceX turned a heralding moment for Starship into its greatest
Crew-13 carried NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. NASA had projected a docking around 8 p.m. ET, as Teslarati reported the day before launch , and Dragon arrived nearly an hour early. Our launch day coverage noted that the flight was lined up to be the quickest Crew Dragon transit yet.
The speed came from timing more than hardware. SpaceX’s Julianna Scheiman said the station “was in an opportune spot in space,” which let Dragon start closing the gap almost immediately after reaching orbit. “This is close to the fastest it could be,” she added. Most Crew Dragon flights still take close to a day, using a series of Draco thruster burns to raise and phase their orbit before arrival.
Dragon’s next job at the station is a departure. NASA said Monday it is targeting 8:05 a.m. ET on Wednesday, October 7, for Crew-12 to undock, setting up a splashdown off the coast of California around 11:34 a.m. on Thursday. Clearing that port makes room for CRS-35, a cargo Dragon carrying the final set of iROSA solar arrays.
Dragon remains NASA’s only operational ride to the station while Boeing’s Starliner stays grounded, and the agency recently added Crew-15, Crew-16 and Crew-17 to SpaceX’s contract in a $946 million modification.

Elon Musk has acknowledged that early discussions with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) could bring the company into his ambitious Terafab semiconductor project, signaling a possible partnership with the world’s leading contract chipmaker.
Musk confirmed that early talks are underway, but as of right now, they are “just discussions.” There is no confirmation of a deal nor dismissal of the possibility of one, leaving open the prospect of one of the largest advanced-chip collaborations under discussion in the U.S.
@wholemars Just discussions, but something may come of it
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 3, 2026
The report that speculated on potential discussions between Terafab and TSMC comes from Tim Culpan, who outlined a few ways the collaboration could operate. One is TSMC using the project as an “anchor customer” for future facilities in Texas, potentially contributing process expertise, operational know-how, or capacity while Terafab provides capital, long-term purchase commitments, or both.
Tesla and SpaceX jointly developed the Terafab project, with Intel already participating on the tech side. Elon Musk announced the project in March , and it intends to produce more than one terawatt of AI compute capacity annually once fully built.
Elon Musk’s Terafab project locks up massive new partner
Company statements place the first phase at approximately $16.8 billion in cost, with later filings pointing to a total that could reach well into the tens of billions across multiple stages.
Intel joined the effort in April 2026 and is expected to supply its 14A manufacturing process for the full-scale plant.
Musk has said existing suppliers, including Samsung and TSMC, remain important for near-term needs; Tesla already has production arrangements with Samsung for AI5 and AI6 chips, but that future demand from Optimus robots, Cybercab vehicles , and planned space-based data centers will eventually exceed what the global industry can currently deliver.
Terafab is positioned as the long-term answer to that projected shortfall, and Tesla did something similar during COVID to avoid a chip shortage. This is just a much larger-scale solution.
If the partnership were to materialize, it would add TSMC’s industry-leading strategies to a project that already combines Tesla’s and SpaceX’s capital and offtake with Intel’s process technology. For now, the only public confirmation is Musk’s brief acknowledgement that conversations are occurring.
Tesla’s early strategy for charging units operating within its Robotaxi fleet reveals that the company surely has not lost any of that scrappy DNA that took it from an unlikely success story to the most valuable carmaker in the world.
An observer at a Tesla Supercharger in Austin spotted ten total Robotaxi vehicles arrive: one Cybercab and nine Model Y units. A Tesla employee was waiting at the lot and allowed each unit to park itself; every car that arrived had nobody in it.
Tesla wins FCC approval for wireless Cybercab charging system
The Tesla employee would walk around and plug each car in, adjusting the parking if needed:
So look at what I found. This is how Tesla charges unsupervised robotaxis at a public supercharger. Here is a driverless Cybercab showing up with no one in it. There are 9 other Model Ys that showed up too. A Tesla employee is walking around and plugging each of them in. She also moves the cars if they are not positioned well enough to charge. I love this process. One person charges multiple robotaxis at once
— Abhimanyu Yadav (@WorldlyReviewer) October 3, 2026
It’s a very interesting strategy, but extremely understandable at this early point in the Robotaxi program. It’s only been out for about 15 months, and Cybercab just entered the fleet in early September.
On top of that, Tesla is still working tirelessly on its wireless charging apparatus, and a new patent was just published regarding that product last week.
However, this is just another example of how Tesla still has plenty of that scrappy DNA leftover from the “production hell” days , when CEO Elon Musk slept on the floor of the factory, employees were working crazy hours, Tesla was building Sprung Structures to build cars in, and the company was tiptoeing on the brink of bankruptcy.

For now, Tesla is utilizing a simple system for recharging its ride-hailing vehicles, and that is a Tesla employee doing it manually until another solution presents itself. Sure, it’s not the most high-tech thing, and it certainly is not what people might have expected at this point in time, but it works, and it’s keeping the entire suite running.

articles.title_orig: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
articles.title_zh: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has approved the death by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army officer convicted of carrying out a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, an army base in Texas.
The move, if it proceeds, will revive executions in the army, which has not carried one out since 1961.
Death sentences, as well as executions in the US military, are rare and require presidential approval.
Under the army’s code of military justice, premeditated murder does carry the death penalty, but the process is often strict and prolonged.
However, the Trump administration has shown more willingness to seek death penalties for serious crimes, including against civilians.
Here’s what we know about the case:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had initially recommended an execution order for Hasan, and Trump has now approved it, according to an X statement posted by Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.
Parnell said the time and date of the execution will be set by Army Secretary Adam Telle, who is serving in an acting capacity.
“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” he wrote.
On November 5, 2009, the US-born army major, Hasan, a psychiatrist in the force, walked into an army processing centre in Fort Hood, shouted “Allahu Akbar” (God is great) and opened fire on fellow staff members waiting to get medical attention.
Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier, and 32 others were wounded during 10 minutes of shooting. Analysts have called it the worst shooting at a US military base targeting members of armed forces.
Hasan was shot several times after two officers engaged him and remains paralysed from the waist down.
Hasan was immediately court-martialled, and military prosecutors, from the start, sought the death penalty against him.
However, the process would play out over the course of several years even after his conviction – largely because the US military is averse to capital punishment.
During the trial, Hasan represented himself and admitted to the attacks, saying he was trying to stop deployments to Afghanistan and the killing of his fellow Muslims. He was due to be deployed weeks later.
Investigations revealed Hasan had exchanged emails with Yemeni-American scholar Anwar al-Awlaki, accused of ties to al-Qaeda, before the shooting. He had also repeatedly voiced opposition to the US wars in Iraq and Afghanistan to colleagues and the treatment of Muslims in the army.
Hasan made little effort to defend himself, and his assigned lawyers claimed his testimony aided the opposing side.
He was charged and convicted on 13 counts of premeditated murder in 2013, and jurors recommended the maximum sentence of death. Controversially, Hasan was charged with “workplace violence” because the military justice code does not address the crime of “terrorism”.
The judgement was further delayed by appeals mandated by the military, not because Hasan sought them.
In 2020, the US Army Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the death penalty for Hasan, and in 2023, the US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces did the same. In March 2025, the US Supreme Court denied a mandatory petition for a judicial review.
In September 2025, Hegseth announced he was seeking presidential approval for Hasan’s execution.
At the time, there was no report of Hegseth specifically seeking death by firing squad.
The president holds the ultimate authority to specify the designated method of execution.
Other forms of execution could have been lethal injection or hanging, which the US military has used in the past.
While Trump’s approval will begin a series of steps towards preparing for the execution, Hasan can still put the process on hold for years with an appeal in the civilian federal court system.
However, that might be unlikely as Hasan made no effort to defend himself during the trial.
He has been remanded to the US Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas, where three other men have also been on the military death row for years.
Among them is Hasan Akbar, convicted of two counts of murder after attacking fellow army members on a Kuwait base in 2003, during the invasion of Iraq.
Another is the convicted serial killer and rapist Ronald Gray, who was found guilty of four counts of murder and eight counts of rape in 2008. He was approved for execution in the same year under President George W Bush, but the process was put on hold by a judge.
Timothy Hennis, a former sergeant, was convicted in 2010 of a triple murder and is also on death row.
The last military execution took place in 1961, when former soldier John Bennett was hanged for the rape of an 11-year-old girl.

articles.title_zh: Chapel Intern gains global finance experience at World Bank Treasury
articles.content_orig:
Daniel Garcia Calao spent the summer gaining experience in global finance through a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury in Washington, D.C. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — When Daniel Garcia Calao came to Penn State from Bogotá, Colombia, he hoped earning a college degree in the United States would open new opportunities. Four years later, his Penn State journey has taken him from Penn State Abington to Penn State University Park and, most recently, to Washington, D.C., for a summer internship with World Bank Treasury.
Garcia Calao, who is dual majoring in economics and finance with a minor in supply chain and information systems , spent the summer completing a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury . There, he worked with three teams, gaining experience in pensions, asset and liability operations, and advisory services.
“It was a truly global experience that strengthened both my technical skill set and my understanding of international financial institutions,” Garcia Calao said.
As a Chapel Executive Intern , Garcia Calao received enrichment funding through the Liberal Arts Career Enrichment Network to help cover his housing expenses in Washington. He also enrolled in LA 495 Undergraduate Field Experience, a half-credit course designed to help students reflect on and make the most of their internship experiences.
“The Chapel Executive Internship made the summer possible,” Garcia Calao said. “The funding covered my summer housing, which allowed me to save and invest my money and work toward my financial future.”
Garcia Calao was born and raised in Colombia and began his Penn State experience at the Abington campus. As an international student adjusting to a new environment, he found community through campus involvement, eventually serving as president of the Latine Student Organization and participating in student government and Lion Ambassadors .
After two years, he transitioned to the University Park campus, where he continued building his network and pursuing leadership opportunities.
Garcia Calao’s interest in economics and finance continued to grow as he progressed through Penn State. He added economics as a second major to broaden his knowledge and strengthen his preparation for internships and a career in finance. Courses in microeconomics, statistics and environmental economics gave him experience with concepts that he later encountered at World Bank Treasury, including central banking, economic policy and how different economies operate.
Daniel Garcia Calao explored Washington, D.C., while living and working in the city as a Chapel Executive Intern during summer 2026. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Networking also played a major role in helping Garcia Calao find his internship. His path to the World Bank began after attending a Penn State Global Careers Institute event where a Penn State alumnus who worked at the World Bank spoke.
Garcia Calao reached out to the alumnus after the event to learn more, and that conversation helped introduce him to an organization where he had never pictured himself working.
“The whole reason I applied to the World Bank was because of that event,” Garcia Calao said. “Attend events because you never know what opportunities will arise. I wouldn’t have seen myself working at the World Bank before that.”
After getting an interview, Garcia Calao continued using networking to prepare. He reached out to professionals through LinkedIn, including one connection who eventually became a mentor. Those conversations helped him prepare for his interview, better understand the World Bank and think about what he wanted to do after graduation.
He said his favorite rotation was in the pensions department. Because he previously completed an investment internship, he was familiar with some of the work and felt he could demonstrate the skills he had developed. He worked on two projects and was able to see how his work continued to progress after his rotation ended.
“Sometimes interns can feel like the work they’re doing isn’t important,” Garcia Calao said. “Seeing how something I worked on progressed showed me that the work I did provided value to the team.”
Garcia Calao said his international background became an asset during an internship that brought him into contact with colleagues from around the world. Fluent in Spanish and Italian, he was able to draw on his language skills and experience navigating different cultures.
“Being able to communicate properly with people across the world is important,” Garcia Calao said.
Daniel Garcia Calao, middle row, fourth from right, joins fellow World Bank Treasury interns following their final capstone presentation. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Thanks to the Chapel Executive Internship Program, Garcia Calao was able to live right in Washington rather than having to find less expensive housing farther away. Living in Washington also gave Garcia Calao the opportunity to experience the city beyond his internship. He stayed in George Washington University housing, managed his daily commute and explored museums and monuments with fellow interns.
Daniel Garcia Calao participates in the D.C. SCORES tournament while living and working in Washington, D.C., during his summer internship. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
After he graduates this fall, Garcia Calao will join the pensions department at the World Bank where he completed part of his internship. He said he also hopes to eventually attend graduate school.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Attack aircraft, military vehicles visible at new China-Laos base, satellite images show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Attack aircraft, military vehicles visible at new China-Laos base, satellite images show
articles.content_orig:
China has opened a new military training and logistics facility in Laos , extending Beijing's security presence deeper into mainland Southeast Asia and potentially giving the Chinese air force its first dedicated foothold overseas.
The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport, north of the capital Vientiane, formally began operations late last month alongside the new China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
Beijing says the center will primarily help train Lao air force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by the two countries.
The opening adds to China's still relatively small network of overseas military facilities.
Beijing established its first foreign military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in 2017. A Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base was formally inaugurated last year, giving Chinese forces access to a facility strategically positioned near the South China Sea.
Laos and Cambodia are widely regarded as China's closest political partners in Southeast Asia, and military cooperation with both has expanded substantially in recent years.
"The two institutions … are not directed against any third party and aim to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region," said the Chinese Defense Ministry in a public statement.
The facility's infrastructure gives Beijing the option of expanding its military use in the future, Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at Australia's Lowy Institute, told DW.
"The focus may well be on joint training, but it has the potential to become a more permanent base. Should Beijing choose to use it as such, it has ample political leverage over Vientiane to demand exclusive access in the future," he added.
Laos has become heavily dependent on Chinese investment and financing during the past two decades. Critics have frequently accused Beijing of engaging in "debt-trap diplomacy."
The International Monetary Fund estimates Laos' public debt at around 81% of GDP last year, with China by far the largest bilateral creditor.
In 2020, China's state-owned China Southern Power Grid acquired a reported 90% stake in Electricite du Laos Transmission Company, which operates much of Laos' electricity transmission network.
A more durable Chinese military presence in Laos would also add another dimension to the strategic competition between Beijing and Washington in Southeast Asia.
The United States still enjoys far more extensive military access across the wider Indo-Pacific, particularly through alliances with the Philippines, Japan and Australia .
Beijing has historically lacked comparable overseas facilities. But Ban Keun, alongside Ream, could gradually reduce that disadvantage by giving the Chinese military additional locations from which to train, maintain equipment and potentially preposition supplies.
It is a particularly ominous development for Vietnam , Euan Graham, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Hanoi and Beijing retain close party-to-party and economic relations, but they remain rivals in the South China Sea , where their competing territorial claims have repeatedly generated tensions.
Vietnam has also traditionally viewed Laos and Cambodia as strategically important buffers along its western flank and has worked for decades to maintain considerable political and military influence in both countries.
"Hanoi has always perceived the Indochinese peninsula as within its sphere of influence, offering a buffer against external aggressors, especially given Vietnam's narrow midriff," said Graham. "Now, it faces an alarming possibility of strategic encirclement by China. The new air base in Laos will certainly complicate Vietnam's defense planning."

Other analysts caution, however, that geography places clear limits on Ban Keun's military value.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told DW that China could gradually expand its presence at the facility.
Beijing could deploy more personnel, particularly advisers and instructors, as well as trainer aircraft and eventually more advanced aircraft, while also using the site to preposition equipment and supplies, he said.
But the "operational usefulness for the PLA's projection of military power in Southeast Asia is constrained by the landlocked nature of Laos."
Unlike Ream, Ban Keun provides no sea access, while Chinese military aircraft already operate from substantially larger and better-equipped bases in southern China.
While Vietnam will closely monitor Ban Keun for its potential role in any future South China Sea conflict, the site's geography doesn't give the Chinese military a significant operational advantage, said Koh.
Simon Creak, an associate professor at Singapore's National Institute of Education and a historian of Laos, noted that Vientiane has maintained a policy of non-alignment since adopting its current foreign policy in 1986.
"It has not had similar joint facilities in the past despite boasting close political and military relations with Vietnam, as well as China and Russia … and any mention of foreign bases in Laos typically recalls the CIA's bases during the Indochina Wars," Creak said.
Still, he believes it's "highly unlikely" that Laos will adjust its formal foreign policy settings or its longstanding effort to balance relations with Vietnam, Thailand and China.

articles.title_zh: “The Good Society and the Inner World” at Thirty-Five
articles.content_orig:
The first chapter of sociologist Michael Rustin’s The Good Society and the Inner World opens autobiographically, positioning its author at the interstices of two possibly incommensurable worlds.
I have regarded myself for many years as a socialist,” Rustin begins. “For a lesser number of years, I have also been considerably influenced by psychoanalytic ideas of a largely Kleinian kind, through reading, through a personal analysis, and through a continuing acquaintance with my wife’s work as a psychotherapist. The issue is: what, if any, is the relationship between these two powerful perspectives? Are they compatible or not? Do they tend in the same or in inconsistent directions? This issue perhaps has a more than personal interest.
When Rustin speculates that his predicament might hold “more than personal interest,” he is surely being modest. Attempts to “braid” Marx and Freud, remarks historian Hannah Zeavin, may often result in “a failed braiding,” but “failure is not only bad, it can be productive,” holding out the prospect of a “unified theory of unhappiness, not so ordinary, but also ordinary.” There remains for many of us an abiding sense that both projects need something from the other: that the Left needs more complex understandings human subjectivity in overcoming economism and didacticism, and that the premise of free association remains more radical than many dominant incarnations of psychoanalysis can permit. For some, Rustin’s assertion that “It is still an open question, in the case of psychoanalysis, what its ultimately most important political affiliations will be,” may prove too generous to psychoanalysis. And yet that very assertion also keeps open the possibility of Zeavin’s productive failures.
Many efforts to hold these worlds in tension work with Freud or Lacan, reading these prolific and ever-evolving thinkers for their self-contradictions and against their sometimes-bourgeois inclinations. Other worthy efforts refuse Eurocentric genealogies of psychoanalysis altogether, as does psychologist Lara Sheehi in her remarkable recent book, From the Clinic to the Streets , which instead begins with the revolutionary Martinican psychiatrist Frantz Fanon.
But Melanie Klein’s is a name that comes up somewhat less often in efforts to forge a Left psychoanalysis. Born in Vienna in 1882, Klein spent the better part of her career in London, where she moved in 1926, and was a leading figure in what became known as the British object-relations school of psychoanalysis until her death in 1960. Among what psychologist Janet Sayers memorably called the “mothers of psychoanalysis,” Klein inspired second-wave feminists like the sociologist Nancy Chodorow, and has more recently become influential in queer studies, where her core concept of reparation continues to elicit considerable controversy via the work of literary scholar Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick . Yet explicitly socialist engagements with Klein’s work, like Rustin’s, remain somewhat rare. [1]
The Good Society and the Inner World turns thirty-five years old this month – an age that also comprises the threshold for both the current medical definition of advanced maternal age and eligibility for election to the U.S. presidency. Given Klein’s abiding interest in the mother-child dyad as a formative scene of psychic life and Rustin’s curiosity about “the social and political affiliations of Kleinian psychoanalysis,” perhaps thirty-five years marks an apt, more than coincidental occasion to revisit this book. Although Rustin is focused on psychoanalytic institutions and Left politics in Britain, I invoke the U.S. presidency, tongue firmly in cheek, to mark my own curiosity as an American socialist with a longstanding interest in Klein about how Rustin’s insights might travel across space as well as time. Accordingly, it is to his political essays, which comprise the first third of the book, that I devote most attention.
[book-strip index="1" style="buy"]
Rustin turns to Melanie Klein in search of a more layered, social view of the human subject, seeking an alternative to both a too-neat Left social constructivism and the neoliberal individualist accounts of human nature on the ascendant in the age of Thatcher. In Rustin’s view, what distinguishes the Kleinian school from other psychoanalytic traditions is its emphasis, informed by Klein’s clinical observations in play therapy with children, on human subjectivity as “the emergent result of a prolonged and delicate process of dependency.”
For Klein, dependence means we are relational creatures from the start—and crucially, that relationality is hardly a uniformly benign, cuddly affair. In Klein’s “distinctively uncompromising view of human destructiveness,” Rustin explains, the terrifying fact of initial dependence gives rise to an infant’s destructive, often unconscious feelings of aggression, envy, greed, and rage toward a phantasy image of the primary caregiver – the first “object” in “object-relations.” At pains to make sense of contradictory, incoherent sensations and feelings, the infant struggles to imagine that caregiver as a whole, separate, imperfect being, instead idealizing some parts of the caregiver as beneficent while reviling others as corrupt and persecutory. In Klein’s lexicon, this frantic splitting exemplifies the “paranoid-schizoid” psychic position. Gradually, and never completely, infants come to reconcile these bifurcated images with their caregivers’ reality—to take responsibility for their aggression and fashion a more realistic unconscious image of a flawed but loved whole object. Klein calls this process “reparation,” which can only be successfully undertaken from a different, “depressive” psychic position. Rustin thus identifies “a hopefulness in the Kleinian account”. Dependence on others engenders hostility and destructive envy, but also remorse, concern, and love. We live with the tension between those (mostly unconscious) feelings – between the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions – throughout our lives.
Presented with this capsule account, it is both unsurprising and understandable that Klein and her followers are sometimes criticized for an overly essentialist, universalizing, and biological view of the human. Klein effectively displaced the primacy of the Oedipal “mommy-daddy-me” triad familiar to readers of Freud, a move that continues to inform feminist and queer interest in her work. But her shift in emphasis to the mother-child relationship as the crucible of human development—a point on which classical Kleinians could be quite doctrinaire—risks inscribing its own particular scene of kinship and gendered labor as definitive of all humanity. Many who build on Klein emphasize the openness of “mothering” as a category to people of all genders, and I used “primary caregiver” above in that spirit. But insofar as these tweaks in language still assume an ideal, natural form of kinship from which some might deviate, they are surely inadequate in and of themselves, as Judith Butler has pointed out .
And yet Rustin models an approach to Klein that seeks not so much a one-size-fits all model of kinship as insight into dependence as a psychic predicament that is at once socially contoured and inexorable. “The task of providing care, membership and identity in society,” he advises, “plainly cannot be met through the restoration of some religious or ideological myth of the family” (38). Instead of a “regressive” renewal of the family romance, he calls for a creative political extrapolation from Klein’s work, such that “commitments to the processes of familial relationship found in object-relations… enrich socialist ideas of what should be asked of wider relationships and institutions” (38). articles.title_orig: What happened during Christa Pike's failed execution
articles.title_zh: What happened during Christa Pike's failed execution
articles.content_orig:
Public radio reporter Catherine Sweeney, one of the media witnesses, recounts the moments before the execution of Christa Pike was halted last Wednesday, Sept. 30.  (AP Photo/George Walker IV)   Flanking the podium are two photos of Colleen Slemmer, Pike's victim in the 1995 murder. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Last week, I was one of the seven media witnesses who observed Tennessee fail to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in almost 200 years.
This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News .
From our previous reporting , each of us had an inkling that the lethal injection process might not go according to plan.
Pike's attorneys had asked the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow her to be hanged instead , citing concerns that a platelet disorder and small veins would make the actual injection not only painful but ineffective.
And Tennessee had already botched an execution attempt in May, when healthcare workers failed to establish complete IV access into Tony Carruthers, who was sentenced to death after being convicted for his involvement in the kidnapping and murders of three people in 1994.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said after the failed execution of Carruthers, who has maintained he is innocent, the state wouldn't try again to kill him for at least a year. After Pike left the execution chamber in an ambulance on Sept. 30, Lee announced he would suspend lethal injections for the rest of the year.
The morning of Pike's scheduled execution, I and the other media witnesses arrived at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville by 8:30 a.m. and waited to be ushered into the prison with nothing but our driver's licenses in hand. The plan was to wait inside until Pike began her journey to the death chamber at 10 a.m.
But we didn't make it that far.
Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Before the Department of Correction's staffers began moving us away from the outdoor media tent and our belongings, the reporters' phones all went off. A federal circuit court had stayed the execution. This was my fifth stint as a media witness to an execution, and I'd never seen a stay issued. We didn't know what that would mean.
It turned out to mean waiting for nine hours at the prison, barred from leaving the grounds. We spent most of it in the boardroom where parole hearings take place.
Throughout the wait, the victim's family often came up in conversation. In 1995, Pike, then 18 years old, killed Colleen Slemmer, who was 19. Slemmer's family lives in Florida and traveled to Tennessee for the execution with money raised through crowdfunding. It's unclear where they waited while the last-minute legal wrangling played out.
Sometime around 6 p.m., the prison system's communications director, Dorinda Carter, told us: "It's a go."
Media witness Catherine Sweeney speaks during a news conference at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted on Sept. 30. George Walker IV/AP hide caption
Tennessee had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to lift the stay, and it did. Carter read the ruling aloud to us.
For unknown reasons, it took another hour or so for the security team to usher us into the witness bay, an all-white cinderblock room with black pleather chairs in two rows and a big window overlooking the death chamber. A loudspeaker pipes sound into the room from the chamber when the microphones are on.
A black curtain hangs in front of the window inside the death chamber. Department of Correction workers open it once IV lines are inserted into the condemned prisoner.
The curtain is there to obscure the workers who place the IVs, in order to shield their identities as required by state law. That process is enshrined in the "Lethal Injection Execution Protocol," which is the guidebook the Department of Correction writes for itself. There is no other regulation over executions in the state.
My employer, the Nashville public radio station WPLN, is a party in a lawsuit challenging the state's concealment of the IV insertion. When executions are botched, it's often due to something going wrong while IVs are placed — or with the subsequent step if IVs fail, placing a central line in a deeper vein through the chest, neck, or groin.
A lower court ruled in favor of WPLN and other media plaintiffs in January, but the state appealed the order, and it has been halted while higher courts consider the case.
The American Medical Association officially bars doctors from participating in executions, and many other health professionals also consider assisting an execution to be unethical.
Outside of prison staffers and the execution team, only the prisoner's spiritual adviser and attorney are allowed in the room with the prisoner while the IVs are inserted. So generally, attorneys' descriptions are the only account of the procedure.
Under normal circumstances, witnesses sit in the bay for 10 or 15 minutes with the curtain closed. That's how long it tends to take for the IV team to place a line and start running saline, to prepare for the 5 grams of the sedative pentobarbital that will be pumped in to kill the prisoner.
Once the lines are set, the execution team enters an adjacent, concealed room. The IV lines run through the wall into that hidden chamber, from which the drugs are administered.
But at Pike's execution, we sat in the bay for 45 minutes with the curtain closed and the microphone turned off.
Until Carruthers' failed execution, the Department of Correction kept the lights off in the witness bay during the wait. Witnesses at his execution said they sat in a dark room for an hour and a half as the execution team tried and failed to place an IV line. This time, the prison kept the lights on.
The clock we use to give a minute-by-minute account is in the death chamber, so we can't see it with the curtain closed. John North, a reporter with the television station WBIR in Knoxville, was the only witness wearing a watch. The rest of us asked him over and over what time it was.
After half an hour, it was clear the IV team must have been struggling.
We wondered whether Pike's execution would unfold similarly to Carruthers'. That time, the governor called and ordered the execution halted before the curtain ever opened.
But at 7:27 p.m., we heard the curtain being drawn away.
We saw Pike in profile, lying on the gurney, facing the window for the other bay, where the victim's family and prosecutors sit.
We saw Pike's spiritual adviser, Mikey Noechel , who wore a wine-red sash over his suit. Together, they sang and talked about Buddhist teachings.
Under the state's protocol, the spiritual adviser is allowed in the death chamber as the pentobarbital flow begins, though the attorneys are not.
There is no signal when the lethal drugs start flowing, but it's assumed to begin after the prisoner delivers her final words. It's typical for the spiritual adviser to offer prayers and other support, and for there to be a back-and-forth between the two.
"I just want to say that I'm going to leave this world the way I've spent most of my life, and that is with love," she said.
She said that she had love for those who hate her, and that she was at peace with her death.
Moments later, Pike told Noechel her arm was burning. She said it was in one specific spot and asked corrections staff in the room whether that was normal.
Pentobarbital is alkaline, so it burns like drain cleaner if it touches skin. If the IV is administered correctly, that is unlikely to happen.
But Pike and Noechel chatted for what seemed a shocking amount of time. Prisoners tend to show signs of being sedated a few minutes in. Pike didn't.

Risks tied to global conflicts, inflation and artificial intelligence pose "growing concerns" to the industry and the state, the comptroller's office said.

Nvidia stock is approaching a $6 trillion market capitalization, a threshold no company has reached, according to Bloomberg .
Nvidia stock has risen 28% this year, pushing its market cap to just below $5.8 trillion, and no other company has done more to lift the S&P 500's 14% advance in 2026, according to Bloomberg.
Two developments have driven the rally, according to Bloomberg: a strong revenue outlook from the company and an authorization of an additional $150 billion under its existing share-repurchase program, which Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said "reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead." Huang has also called Nvidia "the world's first and only growth value stock."
"Nvidia is attractive on both a growth basis and a value basis, and it looks like a haven from any damage higher rates could do to the economy," Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors, which owns Nvidia stock, told Bloomberg. "All of which makes it such an attractive proposition here and a place people should continue to gravitate to if they have concerns."
Larry Tentarelli of Blue Chip Daily said that as the prospect of Federal Reserve rate hikes has become more concrete, capital has been flowing into large-cap technology names seen as relatively insulated from rising borrowing costs. He also pointed to Meta Platforms' Muse AI agent as a catalyst behind a broader recovery in semiconductor stocks. "Big rotation back into semis, a big rotation back into the megacaps and both of those play out well for Nvidia," Tentarelli said.
The rally is all the more striking given that Nvidia shares were still 11% in the red as recently as March 30, a period when doubts about the return on AI infrastructure spending were running high, according to the outlet. The mood has since reversed, with public discourse moving away from whether AI is commercially viable and toward deeper concerns about what the technology means for society.
Nvidia's push toward the $6 trillion threshold comes alongside a significant expansion of its financial footprint across the AI sector. Nvidia's equity investments in AI companies reached $99 billion as of late July , up from roughly $7 billion a year earlier, with the company committing more than $40 billion in 2026 alone to frontier AI labs, infrastructure providers, and photonics companies. Nvidia also agreed to acquire open-source AI model platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.
