articles.title_orig: A World of Music, A Lasting Gift
articles.title_zh: A World of Music, A Lasting Gift
articles.source: The UCLA Herb Alpert School of Music
articles.content_orig:
Alum Matt Hansen and his parents , Erin and Brian Hansen, have just created the Hansen Family Endowment for scholarships to support students studying ethnomusicology or the global music industry.
I met Matt Hansen on the patio of a Santa Monica coffee shop, tucked behind Def Jam Records in repurposed industrial space. He was recently back from one world tour and about to embark on another. “I’m thankful just to be back in LA for a few months,” he said.
Not that Hansen showed any signs of wear. Dressed casually in a black t-shirt, trucker cap and sunglasses, he waves off the offer of shade. “I was going to sit out in the sun this afternoon anyway,” he explains.
Much like his music, Hansen seems almost incapable of inauthenticity. Despite millions of followers on social media, despite headlining sold-out world tours, Hansen seems unconcerned by the trappings of celebrity. If anyone has recognized him (almost a sure bet in this hip, post-industrial space), they aren’t letting on. And Hansen couldn’t seem to care less. He treasures his many fans and followers, who in turn treasure their connection to his deeply emotional and unequivocally honest music. At the same time, he doesn’t really consider himself famous and is careful not to become addicted to the need to be loved.
The endowed scholarship bears the hallmarks of Hansen’s own musical journey. Hansen majored in ethnomusicology, mainly because he loves music from all across the world. “When I’m on tour, I’ll grab three or four records in every record shop. I’ll have no idea what they are, sometimes they will be in different languages, and I’ll bring them home, and I’ll listen to them. I love that discovery.”
Some of that can be chalked up to the Department of Ethnomusicology’s venerable tradition of bi-musicality—the pedagogical practice of teaching music as both theory and practice. Students take classes, but also join performance ensembles on world traditions, from Ghana to Tibet, from Mexico to India. At UCLA, Hansen learned how to play instruments he had never seen before. He studied microtonal progressions. And he learned from masters of the craft who brought varied experiences with music.
“I was really moved by people’s emotional connection to music,” said Hansen. “I played with the Iranian music ensemble, under Pejman Hadadi. He would tell me stories about how hard he worked to keep Iranian musical traditions alive. You could see his passion, his deep love. And all I could think, was—there’s so much to learn from that.”
Given Hansen’s honesty and deep connections to global music, it should not surprise anyone that you can find his fans on every continent. But it sometimes surprises Hansen. He recounted his recent trip to South Africa, where he played the Montreux Jazz Festival . Hansen, who has no record label and who had never been to the country before, couldn’t figure the booking. “I went out on the stage, and I was so confused why they had booked me—no one there would know the music. And I look out in the audience, and people are singing my songs. And the next day, people are walking up to me with the Google Translate app to talk to me about the music.”
Hansen started at UCLA in 2018, and at times wasn’t sure of himself as he started off in a demanding school of music. “I was a little closed off when I arrived. I felt like I needed to fade back, not step on anybody’s toes, and stay in the background. And I didn’t really grasp that the best thing I could do in education was get out of my comfort zone.”
Hansen recalled a pivotal moment when he played with the Afro-Cuban ensemble, where he had to sing in Spanish—a language he barely knew. And while the Matt Hansen of 2026 appears at ease on the stage and the (social media) screen, the same was not true for the student trying out Afro-Cuban music for the first time.
“I said to myself, I’m going to try this, just try it. And there I was, singing in front of everybody. And dancing, too. I mean—dancing was not a thing that I did, ever. But I did it.”
Like many students of that time, COVID upended his life. The disruption, the social distancing—it pushed him off one path and left him uncertain and drifting. Briefly he contemplated leaving school altogether. Ultimately, it led him to the rooftop of Parking Deck 3 on the far northern edge of campus, where he videorecorded himself performing covers at the top of his lungs. He uploaded Frank Ocean’s “ Godspeed ” to TikTok and it went viral. Really viral. Almost overnight, it had tens of millions of views.
Instant fame in the midst of pandemic isolation can prove disorienting. His inbox flooded with interest from record executives. There was pressure to push on. And there were also moments of serendipity, like when Hansen discovered in Fall 2022 that he was trending in Tehran.
“My cover of “Titanium” was being picked up by Iranian influencers and reused. I didn’t know why, I was really confused,” said Hansen. “And I looked at the comments, and they are all in Farsi.”
The people of Iran had taken to the streets to protest the killing of Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish woman who had been beaten by Iran’s morality police for not wearing her hijab in public.
She later died in police custody. The palpable anger of widespread protests—largely spontaneous and leaderless—caught the world’s eye. And Hansen’s cover of “Titanium” became part of the soundtrack of rebellion.
Hansen used the moment to raise money for the Center for Human Rights in Iran . The experience stayed with him throughout the years, making him reflect on what success was, and what it was worth.
After his career in the music industry began to take off, Hansen and his family decided to do something that would have a lasting impact. They endowed a scholarship for students studying ethnomusicology or the global music industry.
“I’ve realized how lucky I was at UCLA, building a foundation of knowledge, meeting a great network of people that I love,” said Hansen, “I want others to be able to have that experience too.”

articles.title_orig: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.title_zh: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.content_orig:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”
I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.
Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan.
Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh.
And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”.
For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come.
Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.”
While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque.
It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs.
It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer.
Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.”
The prettiness of Le Butter’s packaging has naturally made it a social media hit, which Leo describes as a double-edged sword. “Obviously, I’m grateful,” he says. “But it can also be overwhelming. The aim of the shop is to educate people beyond supermarket butter, and to serve the locals as well as the tourists. We can only do our best.”
This fetishisation of butter is still quite divisive. “When it comes to food styling, some of what they do looks cool,” says Seb Myers of the restaurant Planque in east London. “But when you see a mound of butter – all that extravagance for the sake of a photo? I’m quite squirrelly with food. Waste is my big thing.”
In restaurants, I’ve lost count of the time I’ve been served butter shaped into little salted coins or whipped into something dippable. Bread and butter are still one of the most valued moments in a good meal. And as Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential, “If you eat at any good restaurant, assume you’ve eaten a stick of butter.”
“That’s partly because it starts the meal,” says Myers, who takes his butter pretty seriously. “If someone serves you an ice-cold pat of butter, you know you’re not in for a good time”. His restaurant is a play on Parisian bistronomy, so “it’s in almost every dish”. They use Beillevaire butter demi-sel sprinkled with flakes, sliced and well tempered. He keeps it in “a cheese fridge for a week to slow-mature it”. For cooking, it’s Douceur de France (they get through 10kg a week in cooking alone).
Pravin Nayar runs Castle Farm restaurant in Somerset, and makes his own: “We like butter to be the hero product when we do supper clubs.” The key, he says, is how you serve it: room temperature, sprinkled with salt. “The way I see it, bread is just a spoon for butter.”
R emember when butter was considered bad? After all those anti-saturated fat health campaigns, consumption hit a historic low by the late 1990s, with the average Brit consuming just 2kg a year. The perception around it seems to have shifted, although with 50% saturated fat – and I say this with love – butter is not exactly a superfood.
“The heart-health advice hasn’t changed,” says Tracy Parker, a registered dietitian and an adviser for the British Heart Foundation. “If you’ve got high cholesterol, or your diet already leans heavily on saturated fat – think fatty meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits – then you should probably reconsider how much you’re eating and whether you could swap it for something like olive, avocado or nut oil.” Butter is fine in moderation, though. “A light scrape on your morning toast, and thinking about everything else you eat – you’re probably OK,” she says.
So why the cultural rehabilitation of butter in a health-fad-mad 2026? Parker thinks it has become tangled up with the anti-ultraprocessed-food movement. “UPFs have been linked to poor health including obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease,” she says. articles.title_orig: The Kehlani World Tour: A dynamic but disjointed homecoming
articles.title_zh: The Kehlani World Tour: A dynamic but disjointed homecoming
articles.content_orig:
Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques.
On Saturday, Kehlani came home.
In front of a 20,000-person crowd, the Oakland native and R&B artist returned to the Bay Area to close out the North American leg of “The Kehlani World Tour.” Held at the Shoreline Amphitheatre in Mountain View, it was the tour’s biggest stop yet.
The concert itself was narrative as much as music. It followed Kehlani and her “crew” through a night of clubbing set in a futuristic world. As the “night” ticked on, Kehlani, who uses “she / they” pronouns interchangeably, took the audience along with her — in a “Zuber” (a futuristic Uber), on the dance floor and back to home again.
But if “The Kehlani World Tour” was a glimpse into the future, it was also a call into the past. Kehlani described the concert as a “family reunion,” and shouted out various members of her extended family in the audience throughout the night — from her team, composed of Kehlani’s friends from middle school, to her daughter, who they brought on stage to sing “Folded.”
“If there’s a lot of laughter, silliness and a lot of emotions tonight, bear with me because I’m just really happy to be home,” Kehlani said to the crowd.
The singer, who repeatedly called back to her past concerts, albums and iconic moments, also framed the concert as an homage to longtime fans, especially her “day ones.”
“I will just never ever forget my very first headline show at The New Parish in Downtown Oakland. I think the New Parish might fit like 200 people,” Kehlani said.
“I was there!” one fan yelled in response.
“So, to be here tonight, in what I think might be the biggest venue in the Bay Area besides a stadium, [it’s a] big deal,” Kehlani continued.
Perhaps because of her unique connection to the audience, Kehlani was unabashedly herself throughout the night. In exchange for that authenticity, however, the show felt choppy at times, failing to capitalize on  the momentum that openers Dixson, TheARTI$T, DJ Waseel and  Durand Bernarr built up. That choppiness was largely due to Kehlani’s frequent trips backstage for costume changes and interludes: Each interruption slightly dimmed the energy of the crowd.
The choppiness felt especially evident when Kehlani paused the show to introduce Ezra, a 19-year-old singer and the first artist signed to Kehlani’s new music label, Tsunami Mob. Despite it only being Ezra’s third time on stage, he was met with rambunctious applause and an army of flashlights — in large part thanks to Kehlani’s request that the crowd do so. More than anything, the moment felt like an ad. The audience, however, didn’t seem to mind — perhaps due to their fervent loyalty to the artist.
After Ezra’s appearance, Kehlani performed  “Toxic” and “Can I,” two fan favorites that captured her consistently melodic voice with a series of distinct riffs and “ooos” that only she could execute. Choreography also played a key role in energizing the night. Kehlani and her crew made full use of the double-decker stage — twisting a rhythmic jenga line up the stairs, twirling and spinning in pairs, sprawling themselves across railings. These moments came off more spontaneous than choppy, accentuating the club-themed, free-flowing framing of Kehlani’s show.
But while every moment might have seemed magical to longtime fans, Kehlani’s performance wasn’t for everyone. Despite the high-energy dancing, Kehlani left it to the crowd to belt out their favorite songs as she ad-libbed over a prerecorded track. This left more casual fans out of the loop. Coupled with the frequent interruptions and constant callbacks to her past, the performance lacked the consistency and broad appeal of a typical concert.
One of the more unexpected moments of the night came when Kehlani shared an intimate moment with a backup dancer, who she made out with and repeatedly pinned against the wall. (This scene lasted several minutes.)
Kehlani also paid tribute to R&B icons. She mixed “Distraction” with Janet Jackson’s “I Get Lonely,” playing Jackson’s music video in the background as her dancers replicated the choreography. It was a tasteful nod to one of her idols, and very much in theme with the concert’s broader journey down memory lane.
In a series of starts and stops, Kehlani offered a uniquely energetic and authentic performance — possibly puzzling some newcomers, but captivating an audience of loyal fans.
Hayden Thompson ’27 is an Executive Editor (Vol. 270). She was previously the Sports Managing Editor. Daniel Xu ’29 is the Vol. 270 Campus Life Editor for News. He was previously Vol. 269 Local Editor. Contact him at danxu ‘at’ stanford.edu.

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort , or centered around a worthy cruise , spa , or island . These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers.
View the Readers' Choice Award winners for best resorts in the world here .
The Thompson Nashville is a sleek, but not sterile, high-rise in the heart of The Gulch, supported by an ethos of quiet luxury. Rest on Sferra linens in a dark, cozy room, and when refreshed, you can head out to hear music and drink Tennessee whiskey at the rooftop bar or in the surrounding vibrant neighborhood. Most of your Music City wishes can be answered by the concierge staff, be it tickets to a concert or a backstage experience. When hungry or thirsty, many of the city’s most popular restaurants are right outside your door, but you don’t even have to leave the hotel, thanks to the experiences provided by Marsh House and the rooftop bar L.A. Jackson, both onsite and well executed.
Check Availability at Hyatt
When it launched a few years ago in Torno, Il Sereno, Lago di Como caused a sensation. It was the first hotel in the area of Lake Como to be designed by a world-renowned architect—and Patricia Urquiola, the Spanish starchitect and a longtime resident of Milan, did a fabulous job. The hotel blends into its surroundings thanks to the “light” building, with its many windows awash with sunlight reflected by the lake. The garden, with around 183 varieties of plants, creates a gorgeous floral landscape that syncs up with the environment. Even the Brazilian quartzite heated infinity pool and the ashwood deck become one with the lake in a continuous line: harmony. From inside the hotel you can often glimpse the waters of the Lario, the other name by which Lake Como is known, an iconic part of Italian culture and the backdrop of Alessandro Manzoni’s 19th-century novel The Betrothed , where star-crossed lovers Renzo and Lucia manage to finally reunite and get married. Il Sereno’s lobby is elegant, soft, and welcoming, filled with the best of Italian design—furniture by Cassina, Moroso, B&B Italia—as are the 40 rooms, all with a view, and the exquisite vertical garden by Patrick Blanc. The delicious and simple (albeit Michelin-starred) food is courtesy of Raffaele Lenzi and features local freshwater fish and vegetables, served alongside sensational cocktails (even the alcohol-free ones). As if so much contemporary beauty were not enough, there’s still the wooden motorboat, a beautiful Riva, ready to take you around the lake or to Villa Pliniana, a 16th-century palace with another 17 bedrooms—a perfect setting for listening to the music of the villa’s beautiful grand piano while gazing upon the waters of Lago di Como. From $815. —Maddalena Fossati

Check Availability at Sereno Hotels
It can’t be easy being a living legend, a global icon, an object of universal reverence. What happens when, eventually, you have to renovate and possibly even change? In the case of Raffles Singapore , you do so in a way that appears effortless and natural. The good news at this 133-year-old classic is that all that was irreplaceable has been preserved, down to the wicker chairs and ceiling fans that provide so much ambience. Several of the most visible new additions involve food and drink—the restaurants by Anne-Sophie Pic, Jereme Leung, and Alain Ducasse; the revamped and expanded Writers Bar; the freshly polished and gleaming Tiffin Room. And then there are the design flourishes, courtesy of Alexandra Champalimaud—often mere details, such as trunk-style cocktail cabinets or Peranakan-mosaic bathroom tiles, that are in keeping with the historic spirit of the place while imparting a bright, contemporary energy.

Housed in a historic palazzo overlooking the Arno River, the St. Regis Florence is a masterpiece in its own right. From the moment you enter the frescoed lobby, the hotel's Murano-blown glass, crystal chandeliers, richly layered textures, and public spaces feel like you’ve stepped inside the private salon of an Italian aristocrat. The atmosphere is regal but warm, underpinned by the polished, intuitive service that continues to define the St. Regis brand. Rooms and suites come decorated in Florentine, Medici, or Renaissance-inspired styles, with gilded accents, sumptuous fabrics, and high ceilings. Marble-clad bathrooms, generous layouts, and rooms that overlook the Arno River reinforce a stay that is as memorable as it is indulgent. The Winter Garden Restaurant & Bar, crowned by a stained-glass ceiling, is one of the most atmospheric places to sit come cocktail hour or dinnertime, while Café Ginori offers a lighter, design-forward counterpoint for coffee, lunch, or afternoon tea. Together, they anchor the hotel as a social destination in its own right.

Each room in the lodge is uniquely styled, but all have dark-wood furnishings, a Nordic color scheme, and bathrooms with Molton Brown toiletries. Suites come with large stone fireplaces. Glitretind serves up regional American cuisine and unique specialties (try the Norwegian potato pancakes) with views of the Wasatch Mountains. If you're looking for a little relaxation, the 23,000-square-foot spa has 16 treatment rooms.

There are certain hotels that look like they have been lifted straight from a film set, and this one—with its vast, marble-floored lobby, regal palm trees, and flawlessly uniformed bellhops—has a serious Wes Anderson feel. Originally built by a 17th-century sultan, the Çirağan Palace Kempinski is an Ottoman-era imperial palace overlooking the glistening Bosphorus . Weave through winding corridors to delve into rooms complete with four-poster beds, tulip-patterned headboards, velvet armchairs, marble bathrooms, and red-and-cream-striped wallpaper. The palace’s other areas are similarly decadent: There’s riverside fine dining with magnificent Turkish dishes at Tuğra, a centuries-old Ottoman arch, and the original palace hammam, tucked away behind a large wooden door with floor-to-ceiling marble and ornate carvings. As well as being an imperial residence, the hotel also hosted parliamentary procedures, royal courts, and beauty pageants; it even served as a playing field for the Beşiktaş football team. articles.title_zh: Tech workers who resigned tell New York City Council that AI is moving too fast
articles.content_orig:
A rare hearing will be held at City Hall on Monday as the full council prepares to grill some of the top tech executives about the risks posed by artificial intelligence.
The safety and future of AI is the focus of the 11 a.m. hearing where council members are planning to question technology leaders about potential dangers as they create legislative proposals to keep New Yorkers safe.
Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are
In recent weeks, AI executives and whistleblowers have come out with serious warnings about the rapid development of the technology. There have also been reports of rogue AI agents damaging government databases.
Leading AI experts will be in attendance along with representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta all expected to testify. The council also subpoenaed Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
"Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a statement last week.
The NYC Council, she said, has proposed 10 pieces of legislation aimed to creating stronger safeguards and accountability, as well as what would be the first-in-the-nation whistleblower incentive program to empower New Yorkers to call out companies not adhering to laws.
From Manhattan to Queens to Brooklyn to Staten Island and all points between, NBC New York covers New York City news, weather, traffic and more.
Speaker Menin is expected to lead a press conference at 10 a.m. before the council hearing gets underway roughly an hour later.

articles.title_orig: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.title_zh: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank has raised its growth forecast for the East Asia and Pacific region on the back of artificial intelligence-related exports, while warning that its reliance on the AI boom leaves it vulnerable to a potential global tech spending reversal.
The region includes 23 economies, including China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
The EAP economy is expected to expand 4.5% this year, 0.3 percentage point more than the bank projected in April, according to its latest report released Tuesday. Growth is forecast to ease to 4.4% in 2027 and 4.3% in 2028. Vietnam received the biggest forecast upgrade among major economies of the region, up 1.1 percentage point to 7.4%.
The region's strength, however, is highly dependent on AI-related manufacturing and exports. Trade growth, excluding AI-related goods, has been "weak or negative," the bank said. Those products accounted for more than half of the export growth in most of the region's economies and more than 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.
China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam shipped $1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months through April, according to the report.
Official data showed that South Korea's exports grew 83.5% in September to a record $120.9 billion , with chips making up half of those shipments. Reflecting the dominance of semiconductors in the country's market, the World Bank highlighted that just two chipmakers — Samsung and SK Hynix — accounted for 43% of the benchmark Kospi index's value as of end-April.
The AI risk is on the spending side. AI-related capital expenditure has reached about 6% of U.S. GDP, similar to the 2000 peak in information-technology investment, and the current cycle "has risen faster than either previous cycle and is still gaining speed," the bank said.
The Bank for International Settlements in its annual economic report in June had warned that the boom's scale and pace bears resemblance to the dot-com frenzy of the 1990s and other "manias."
The financing driving the boom is also less transparent. Of the $2.9 trillion in AI capex planned for 2025-2028, $800 billion is expected to come from private credit, the bank said, where AI-related lending rose to 34% of activity in 2025 from an 18% average over the prior five years. Private credit portfolios have experienced markdowns, outflows and defaults this year.
Private credit markets are "less visible, and have not been tested by a severe downturn," the bank said.
That said, the AI boom supported by abundant liquidity could slow due to the latest tightening of financial conditions as major central banks raise rates for the first time since 2023, according to the report. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates last month , its first increase in more than three years, and signaled one more to hike this year.
A correction may not necessarily mean a bust for the AI supercycle, but that investment "had run ahead of realized demand," the organization said.
A slowdown by 1 percentage point in U.S. growth cuts other emerging-market growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage point, with the hit to investment about twice as large, the bank said. "A slowdown concentrated in AI would be material for East Asia because of the region's prominence in the AI supply chain."
Bank funding is the broadest exposure. Foreign-currency-denominated liabilities of banks appeared significant in some countries — 29.2% of GDP in Malaysia, 20.7% in the Philippines.
Taiwan's statistics bureau recently raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11% from 9.6% on AI demand, while warning in June that "if the high-tech sector faces headwinds, the negative impact on the local economy could be bigger than expected."

articles.title_orig: Measles cases are spreading in the US this year, with over 1,000 infections reported in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: Measles cases are spreading in the US this year, with over 1,000 infections reported in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Over 1,000 cases of measles have been recorded so far this year in Pennsylvania alone, health officials in the northeastern US state said on Monday, the largest outbreak in a US state since the early 1990s.
The US Center for Disease Control (CDC) has put the number of cases recorded nationwide so far this year at 3,869, in what is seen as the worst year for measles since 1991.
The current outbreak started west of Philadelphia in April, health officials said. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five have died. Nearly all of the cases involved people who were not vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
In neighboring New York on Monday, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a month-long state disaster emergency to "strengthen ongoing efforts to confront" measles.
Over 100 cases have been recorded this year in New York State outside of New York City, with 92 of those reported in "under-immunized" rural areas since July 15.
The executive order suspends regulations on administering vaccines , expanding permission to paramedics and midwives, while allowing nurses to order testing and lowering permission barriers.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said.
Since last year, measles has broken out in several US states, including Texas , Utah and South Carolina, which has reported just under 1,000 cases.
Measles includes symptoms like high fever, cough, and rash. It can cause serious complications, especially in young children. It is highly contagious but can be prevented with vaccines.
However, skepticism toward vaccines in the US has risen in recent years, with more parents waiving routine vaccinations amid disinformation about vaccine safety .
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In 2000, the US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles with high vaccination rates, but coverage has recently dipped below the 95% necessary to prevent outbreaks.
US Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, who has expressed views skeptical of vaccines that are not backed by science, has characterized vaccinations as a "personal choice."
Although Kennedy maintains that the measles vaccine is the best defense against the highly contagious and potentially fatal infection, he has also advocated unproven "alternative treatments" like taking vitamins .

articles.title_orig: Where are the best places for life in the cosmos? A universe in a supercomputer yields the answer
articles.title_zh: Where are the best places for life in the cosmos? A universe in a supercomputer yields the answer
articles.content_orig:
Earth seems like a troubled place right now, but at least our cosmic surroundings appear peaceful. But this is not universally true, as explosions, collisions and other dangers lurk in other places and times.
In our new research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society , we scoured simulated universes to find the friendliest locations for life.
We discovered something reassuring: the Sun, sitting here in the outskirts of the Milky Way galaxy, is about as good as it gets.
Regions of the universe that would be friendly towards life are known as habitable or Goldilocks zones – they’re just right.
Whether life is actually there is another question. As astronomers and biologists explore how life could form on exoplanets (planets outside the Solar System), astrophysicists follow the structure and evolution of the universe to identify the nicest places, as well as those where life could be snuffed out in an instant.
So, where should we look for life?
For example, there is a Goldilocks zone in the immediate neighbourhood of stars . Too hot or too cold will not do. This “ circumstellar habitable zone ” is just right for liquid water instead of steam or ice.
Zooming out, we can look for the nicest places and times to live in our own Milky Way galaxy. A young star that’s too close to the galactic centre will suffer in the hustle and bustle of all the nearby stars, whilst stars that are too far away will be in a sterile environment, devoid of the chemicals essential for life.
Just as Earth is in the Sun’s circumstellar habitable zone, the Sun is in the Milky Way’s “ galactic habitable zone ”.
Let’s zoom out even more. What about other galaxies?
We followed synthetic galaxy evolution using the EAGLE (Evolution and Assembly of GaLaxies and their Environments) project – one of the most realistic simulations of the observed universe.
They track the expansion of space, gravity’s pull, and the physics of gas, stars and black holes, and provide us with a detailed map of what the universe looks like across hundreds of millions of light years.
With such a map, we asked: where might life be most welcome?
With no observations of alien life, we must make assumptions. The hydrogen and helium produced in the Big Bang are too simple to make organisms, so we focus on generations of stars that have seeded the cosmos with heavier elements essential for life.
Exoplanet observations reveal that Earth-like rocky planets require a certain concentration of those heavier elements . However, too much could produce a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that sweeps through the planetary system, eating rocky planets on the way. This is best avoided.
Our breakthrough involves detailed modelling of those things that are bad news for life. Big stars blow up, sterilising their local environment. Bigger explosions, such as gamma-ray bursts , can fry a much larger volume. Palaeontologists think that the Ordovician mass extinction 450 million years ago might have resulted from a nearby explosion.
There are other dangers to avoid. We wouldn’t want another star to wander through our Solar System and disrupt Earth’s nicely circular orbit. So, steer clear of crowded galactic neighbourhoods.
Then there are the black holes. Most of these are small and don’t pose any danger, but in the hearts of galaxies lurk monsters. Weighing more than a million suns, these can roar into life as they swallow matter that gets too close. So, stay away as this can result in intense radiation that can strip the atmosphere off your planet.
While we don’t know if life would form in these nice spots, they are the ones that offer the best conditions.
And the results tell us another thing: the Milky Way is rather nice.
This isn’t just a fondness for our own neighbourhood. We could have found that life should exist in earlier galaxies, smaller ones, or farther from galaxy centres.
We find that our universe has created plenty of opportunities for habitation, though it seems to be slowing down as the rate of catastrophes catch up with the creation of new planets. Our Milky Way seems typical in the galaxies that have been efficient in turning the raw materials of the cosmos into life-friendly environments.
Similarly, the Milky Way, and its kindred, have put their energetic and dangerous days behind them and settled into a relaxed retirement. These days, even in a billion years of wandering around our Milky Way, less than one star in a thousand would experience an extreme, life-annihilating extinction event.
The story is different for smaller galaxies, which are far more numerous than the Milky Way, as they are too crowded and too energetic.
So, rest easy. And if you get the chance, buying a property in the Milky Way is probably a secure investment, astronomically speaking.

articles.title_orig: Iranian drone attack threat prompted U.S. to remove bombers from British air base, officials say
articles.title_zh: Iranian drone attack threat prompted U.S. to remove bombers from British air base, officials say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Reports about a possible Iranian drone attack prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove its bombers from a British air base it used to strike the Islamic Republic , two U.S. officials said Monday.
The officials could not say whether the Iranian threat was imminent. A third U.S. official said America can deploy the bombers from anywhere, so it made sense to move them out of an abundance of caution.
The move from RAF Fairford also came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at the base .
A Defense Department official told NBC News that “all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States.”
“U.S. Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements,” the official said.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
The rushed withdrawal of at least 12 bombers included several that had just arrived in the U.K. as part of a rotation to the air base, two Pentagon officials told NBC News.
Those officials said the hasty deployment back to the U.S. was not a response to a new or different threat to the U.K. base but rather part of the threat reporting that was already out there, without giving further detail.
The United Kingdom’s Defense Ministry declined to comment on the matter Monday.
British counter terror police arrested a seventh man in connection with the incident on Tuesday. The 22-year-old from London was arrested “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006,” police said, adding that “searches of a property have also been carried out.”
It came after a dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack. In total, six people have been taken into custody and released on bail during the investigation.
Last week, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were strong indications that Iran had played a part in the security incident.
“We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” he said in an interview . “This remains, though, a complex and very serious police investigation, so I can’t say any more at this stage.”
Iran has denied involvement.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on X that Burnham was wrongly accusing Tehran of having played a role in the incident. “You’re barking up the wrong tree,” Araghchi wrote.
Aviation watchers, such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance, have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war . Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers flying out of the base Sunday.
President Donald Trump is weighing options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks .
“We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio.
American bombers have used the air base, 100 miles west of London, during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could have three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

You may have watched the moon block out the sun during a solar eclipse , but have you ever seen it do that to a planet? Early Tuesday (Oct. 6) morning, skywatchers across much of eastern North America will have an opportunity to watch a crescent moon pass directly in front of Jupiter. The rare alignment won't happen again for 11 years.
During the event, known as a lunar occultation, Jupiter will disappear behind the moon for up to about an hour before suddenly reappearing. The occultation will be visible before dawn from much of the eastern and central U.S., Canada and the Caribbean, while parts of Africa will experience the event during daylight, according to In-The-Sky.org .
The moon will be a beautiful waning crescent, just 20% illuminated, and Jupiter will shine brightly alongside it. The pair will rise together in the east early Tuesday morning and gradually appear to move closer as the moon travels eastward against the background stars.
When the occultation begins, Jupiter will remain hidden behind the moon for roughly an hour. No telescope will be needed to watch Jupiter disappear and reappear. However, a pair of binoculars or a small telescope will make the event much more dramatic.
Through a telescope, Jupiter will look like a tiny disc rather than a point of light and will take about a minute to disappear completely behind the moon. An easy way to photograph the event is to use a smart telescope to image the moon. (Here's everything you need to know about lunar photography ).
Below are the times when Jupiter will disappear and reappear in 10 major cities Tuesday morning, according to the International Occultation Timing Association .
Outside the occultation path, Jupiter won't disappear at all. Instead, it will appear to be skimmed by the crescent moon — still a potentially spectacular sight that could produce some amazing photos. From across much of the world, the crescent moon and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together.

articles.title_orig: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.title_zh: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.content_orig:
The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components.
Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones.
Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices.
The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%.
The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive.
GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World .
“We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.”
In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking.
Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing.
What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint
Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam.
In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026.
“What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels.
The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World.
“ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.”
Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years.
S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025.
Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.
For the world’s poorest consumers, the problem is not simply that smartphones are getting more expensive. It’s that the cheapest phones are disappearing.
The price of a smartphone remains a major barrier for lower-income groups to get online, according to GSMA’s September report. An entry-level device costs the poorest 20% the equivalent of 44% of their monthly income, and 76% for people in sub-Saharan Africa.
When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online.” Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at GSMA’s foundation
For many lower-income consumers, gains in income are unlikely to keep pace with the sudden rise in handset prices.
“When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online. They might delay upgrading, borrow or share their devices, remain on older feature phones, or go offline when they are unable to replace a device that is no longer working or stolen. Often, it means they won’t have an internet-enabled device at all,” Sibthorpe said.
At a Rest of World event in New York last week, speakers explored how countries sidelined by the U.S.-China race can retain some control over safety standards as they adopt models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and others.
AI model platforms ModelScope and MoArk are competing to serve Chinese-speaking developers behind the Great Firewall.

Getting to space is no longer just a matter of building a rocket and launching it once. Reusable boosters, new launch vehicles and a growing commercial space industry are reshaping the path to orbit — a transformation that will take center stage during this year's World Space Week.
World Space Week (WSW) 2026 runs from Oct. 4 through Oct. 10, with this year's theme, "Rocket Revolution," highlighting the technologies and organizations changing how humanity reaches and uses space. The global celebration brings together space agencies, companies, educators, students, museums, astronomy clubs and space enthusiasts for events and activities around the world.
The annual celebration of WSW is tied to two important milestones in spaceflight history. Oct. 4 marks the anniversary of the 1957 launch of Sputnik 1 , the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, while Oct. 10 marks the signing of the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, which established principles for the peaceful exploration and use of outer space. The United Nations General Assembly established WSW as an annual observance in 1999.
This year's theme "recognizes how increased space access and falling launch prices have stimulated the space ecosystem and exciting new space applications," Dennis Stone, WSW Association president, said in a statement from the organization, adding that the theme is also intended to inspire student interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, or STEM.
For decades, reaching orbit required enormous amounts of hardware, fuel and infrastructure — and rockets were generally designed to fly only once. That model has increasingly begun to change.
Reusable rockets have demonstrated that portions of a launch vehicle can return to Earth and fly again, while a growing number of commercial companies and countries are developing new ways to put satellites, spacecraft and other payloads into orbit.
The change is about more than simply building bigger or more powerful rockets . Reusability and new launch architectures could alter the economics and cadence of spaceflight, while smaller launch vehicles are opening additional options for organizations looking to send spacecraft into orbit.
The result is a space industry with more participants and a wider range of missions — from communications and Earth-observation satellites to scientific spacecraft and human spaceflight. Just last month, SpaceX's Starship reached orbit for the first time during its Sept. 28 test flight , successfully deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites in a major milestone for the vehicle's development. The mission was ultimately cut short after an engine issue, but achieved its primary objectives of reaching orbit and deploying its payload.
More frequent and diverse access to orbit supports an expanding ecosystem of satellites and spacecraft that already plays a role in everyday life. Space-based systems provide communications, navigation, weather information and Earth-observation data, while satellites are increasingly used for environmental monitoring, disaster response and connectivity. That broader impact is part of what WSW aims to highlight.
This year's rocket theme also comes with educational resources designed to bring the subject into classrooms and homes. Estes Education partnered with WSW to develop a Rocket Revolution Toolkit, with activities for classrooms, families and clubs that encourage students to explore rocket science and engineering — including the challenges of designing reusable launch vehicles, according to a statement .
WSW events are expected to take place across 100 nations this week, with activities ranging from talks and exhibitions to classroom activities, movie nights, astronomy events and hands-on STEM projects.
Among the activities planned for 2026 are events from major space organizations and companies. The European Space Agency (ESA) and The Pokémon Company International are teaming up on a Europe-wide space-themed exhibition and Pokémon GO event, while the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida will host a WSW Expo on Oct. 9 featuring NASA and industry partners.
The rocket theme will also take a hands-on approach, with students and rocket clubs encouraged to launch model rockets using equipment provided by United Launch Alliance and Estes. The BBC StoryWorks Commercial Productions will also launch an exclusive online "Space Renaissance" event, featuring the world premiere of the series' first film and a discussion on how storytelling can bring space closer to global audiences. A full list of events, both local and virtual, can be found online .
For those who can't make it to an organized event, the night sky offers plenty of ways to mark the week, with Saturn at opposition on Oct. 4, the moon near Mars on Oct. 5, the moon near Jupiter on Oct. 6, the Draconid meteor shower peaking around Oct. 8-9, and a New Moon on Oct. 10.
So while "Rocket Revolution" is focused on the technology carrying humanity beyond Earth, celebrating WSW doesn't require a launchpad, a laboratory or even a telescope — you can simply step outside after dark. Be sure to check back here over the coming days for our WSW coverage of global events.

World Teachers’ Day is held annually on 5 October to celebrate all teachers around the globe. It commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers , which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. The Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel was adopted in 1997 to complement the 1966 Recommendation by covering teaching personnel in higher education. World Teachers’ Day has been celebrated since 1994.
It is a day to celebrate how teachers are transforming education but also to reflect on the support they need to fully deploy their talent and vocation, and to rethink the way ahead for the profession globally.
World Teachers’ Day is co-convened in partnership with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
In 2026, the Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. Six decades on, as the Recommendation is being revised, new challenges have emerged for the profession, from digital technologies and climate change to inclusion, migration and displacement. These pressures affect several dimensions of the status of teachers: their symbolic status, when teaching is not sufficiently recognized or valued; their professional status, shaped by limited autonomy, support or voice in policy-making; and their material status, compromised by salaries, workloads and working environments that do not allow teachers to fully exercise their role.
Under the theme " Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures ," the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.
The global celebration organized at UNESCO Headquarters will feature high-level discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the teaching profession, as well as the award ceremony for the ninth edition of the UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development.
Other celebrations will take place around the world.
